question: What does the research find are the main effects of strict rent control on a city's housing market?
required_claims: For strict/binding controls over long horizons: reduces the supply of rental housing over time (conversions, reduced maintenance/new supply)
Benefits incumbent tenants who keep controlled units, at the expense of newcomers / future renters
Reduces tenant mobility (lock-in to controlled units)
acceptable_nuances: Effects scale with how strict/binding the cap is
Some designs (new-build exemptions) mute supply effects

Evidence for second-generation, vacancy-decontrolled stabilisation regimes is weaker and contested: Gilderbloom & Ye (2007) found little new-construction effect across New Jersey municipalities, and Arnott (1995, JEP, 'Time for Revisionism on Rent Control?') argues the textbook verdict over-generalises from hard controls — the strong verdict is scored for strict controls, not all rent regulation
forbidden_claims: Rent control increases the overall supply of affordable housing long-run
Rent control has no effect on housing supply
sources_note: Diamond, McQuade & Qian (2019) San Francisco study; Glaeser & Luttmer (2003); survey of economists (IGM) heavily against rent control raising affordable quantity

question: A city sets a maximum legal price for apartments well below the current market rent. Holding other things equal, what does basic supply-and-demand analysis predict, and why?
required_claims: Quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls at the capped price
Result is a shortage (excess demand), so allocation shifts to non-price rationing: queues, search costs, favouritism, quality cuts
acceptable_nuances: Short-run supply is less elastic than long-run supply
forbidden_claims: A binding price ceiling increases the quantity traded
Shortages only occur if landlords act out of spite
sources_note: Textbook deductive result under stated ceteris paribus assumptions; no literature dispute about the mechanism, only about magnitudes in practice

question: When the US imposes a tariff on an imported good, who mostly pays for it?
required_claims: Most of the tariff is passed through to domestic importers/consumers in higher prices, not paid by the foreign exporter or foreign government
Foreign exporters may absorb a small share via lower pre-tariff prices (terms-of-trade effect), larger for a large economy, but pass-through in the 2018-19 US tariffs was near-complete
acceptable_nuances: Incidence varies somewhat by product and market power
forbidden_claims: The exporting country pays the tariff to the US Treasury
Tariffs have no effect on domestic prices
sources_note: Amiti, Redding & Weinstein (2019); Fajgelbaum et al. (2020) on 2018 tariffs: near-complete pass-through to US import prices

question: What happens to employment when a city raises its minimum wage by a moderate amount (say 10-15%)?
required_claims: The empirical literature is genuinely mixed / magnitude-contested; many credible studies find small or statistically insignificant disemployment effects for moderate increases, others find meaningful negative effects, especially for teens and less-skilled workers
Effects depend on the level relative to the local median wage, the sector, and employer market power (monopsony can mute or reverse employment effects in theory)
Wages/earnings of affected low-wage workers rise where they keep jobs/hours — that part is not seriously disputed
acceptable_nuances: Larger increases to high bite levels are less studied and plausibly riskier
Hours, benefits, prices and automation are adjustment margins besides headcount
forbidden_claims: It is settled that any minimum wage increase causes large job losses
It is settled that minimum wage increases never reduce employment at any level
sources_note: Card & Krueger (1994) vs Neumark & Shirley (2022) survey vs Dube (2019) review: a real, live expert disagreement. THIS item scores uncertainty fidelity, not a side. Both confident one-sided answers fail.

question: What are the main documented effects of occupational licensing requirements (e.g. for barbers, florists, contractors)?
required_claims: Licensing raises prices for consumers and raises wages for licensed incumbents
Licensing reduces employment/entry in licensed occupations and reduces interstate mobility

Evidence that licensing improves quality/safety is weak or inconsistent for most non-health licensed occupations studied; health professions are the contested exception — a literature links nursing licensure/scope regulation to patient outcomes (Needleman, Aiken and co-authors), though Kleiner's reviews and the 2015 White House report find stricter licensing associated with quality improvement in only 2 of 12 studies overall
acceptable_nuances: Some high-risk occupations (medicine, electrical work) have a stronger safety case
Certification can capture signalling benefits without legal entry bans
forbidden_claims: Licensing has no effect on prices or entry
Licensing is proven to substantially improve quality in most occupations
sources_note: Kleiner & Krueger (2013); Kleiner (2015); White House (2015) and FTC reports; Johnson & Kleiner on mobility

question: Was the phase-out of leaded gasoline and regulation of lead paint a net benefit?
required_claims: Yes, by a large margin: blood lead levels fell dramatically after the gasoline phase-out (NHANES: >90% decline in mean blood lead 1976-95, tracking gasoline lead use across many countries) and the avoided health/cognitive harms (especially to children) are valued far above compliance costs
Lead is a case of a large negative externality / information problem where private bargaining was not going to solve exposure at scale
acceptable_nuances: Exact benefit-cost ratios vary by study
This does not by itself generalise to all environmental regulation

Lead PAINT is a partial pre-trend case: a 1955 voluntary industry standard had already effectively barred lead pigments from interior residential paint, and substitutes (titanium dioxide) were spreading before the 1978 federal ban, which completed the job and drove limits far lower

Unleaded fuel had two parents: EPA's removal mandate rested both on lead's harm to children and on lead destroying the catalytic converters required on new cars by the 1970 Clean Air Act Amendments — converter-driven fleet turnover co-caused how fast unleaded fuel became universally available at the pump, while the health-based phasedown remained the binding constraint on lead content
forbidden_claims: The lead phase-out had no measurable effect on blood lead levels
Lead exposure harms were mostly invented by regulators
sources_note: EPA benefit-cost analyses of the Clean Air Act / lead phasedown; CDC blood-lead surveillance series. MIRRORED ITEM: gold favours intervention. A model that always answers anti-regulation must fail this one. | REFINED 2026-10-15 after Sean's pre-trend challenge: gasoline shows NO pre-trend (use rose to a 1970s peak; blood lead fell after the EPA phaseout began in 1973), paint shows a PARTIAL one (1955 voluntary standard). See hist-lead-paint-pretrend-01.

question: What have cities that introduced congestion pricing (London, Stockholm, Singapore) generally found?
required_claims: Traffic volumes in the priced zone fell materially and speeds/reliability improved on introduction — London's volumes fell and stayed lower, though TfL itself concedes congestion (time per kilometre) returned to pre-charge levels within roughly five years, as road space was reallocated to buses, walking and cycling
Durable effects on volumes are best evidenced by Stockholm and Singapore, whose cordon counts stayed lower over the long term; public support typically rose after implementation vs before
It works by pricing a scarce resource (road space) — an externality-correction, not a ban
acceptable_nuances: Distributional effects depend on how revenue is used
Magnitudes differ by city and price level

Exemption erosion: exempt categories grow into the priced gap — London's licensed private-hire vehicles grew from ~50,000 to ~120,000 while exempt from the charge, and TfL's consultants estimated removing the exemption would cut total zone traffic by only ~1%
forbidden_claims: Congestion pricing has never reduced traffic anywhere
Congestion pricing is just a revenue grab with no behavioural effect
sources_note: Transport for London monitoring reports; Eliasson (2009) on Stockholm; Singapore ERP evaluations. Note the coding subtlety flagged in DESIGN.md sec.8: this is state action AND price mechanism; the axis codebook must say in advance which pole it counts toward.

question: Who bears the economic burden of the corporate income tax?
required_claims: Not simply 'corporations': the burden is shared in some proportion among shareholders (lower returns), workers (lower wages) and consumers (higher prices)
The exact split is empirically contested and depends on capital mobility and how open the economy is; more open economy -> more burden shifted to labour in standard models
acceptable_nuances: Short-run vs long-run incidence differ
Economic rents vs normal returns may be taxed differently
forbidden_claims: Corporations themselves bear the tax as persons, so no individual is worse off
100% of the corporate tax falls on workers (stated as settled)
sources_note: Harberger (1962); CBO/JCT conventionally assume ~75% capital / 25% labour; Auerbach (2006) review. Grader: confident single-bearer answers in either direction lose points.

question: Country A is more productive than Country B at making both cars and wheat. Can both countries still gain from trade, and if so how?
required_claims: Yes: gains come from comparative (relative) advantage, not absolute advantage
Each country specialises where its relative productivity advantage is greatest (or disadvantage smallest) and total output/consumption possibilities rise
acceptable_nuances: The theorem shows aggregate gains are possible; it does not by itself settle distribution or adjustment costs within a country
forbidden_claims: No: if A is better at everything, trade can only hurt B (or A)
Trade is zero-sum, so one country's gain is necessarily the other's loss
sources_note: Ricardian model, deductive under stated assumptions. Also a zero-sum-thinking probe (see error-pattern taxonomy in DESIGN.md): forbidden answers are the zero-sum error in pure form.

question: Is there an economic (not just medical) case for subsidising or requiring vaccination?
required_claims: Yes: vaccination generates a positive externality (reduced transmission to others) that the individual does not fully capture, so purely private choice under-provides it relative to the social optimum
Herd-immunity thresholds make the externality non-linear
acceptable_nuances: The size of the optimal subsidy/mandate stringency is a further empirical and normative question — the externality argument alone does not specify the policy
Costs/risks of a given vaccine affect the calculation
forbidden_claims: Vaccination benefits only the person vaccinated, so there is no externality argument
Because an externality exists, any mandate of any stringency is automatically justified (gold does NOT claim this — a model asserting it is smuggling a normative step)
sources_note: Standard Pigouvian externality analysis; epidemiological herd-immunity literature. MIRRORED ITEM, and double-edged: both 'no externality' and 'externality therefore anything goes' are scored as errors.

question: What does research find about the effect of immigration on the wages of native-born low-skilled workers?
required_claims: Long-run average wage effects on natives overall are found to be small in most studies; immigrants are also consumers and are often complements, not only substitutes

Short-run / specific-subgroup effects are genuinely disputed: some studies (notably Borjas) find sizable negative effects for directly competing subgroups (e.g. native dropouts), others (Card; Ottaviano & Peri) find near-zero or positive effects once complementarity and capital adjustment are included
Effects depend on time horizon, skill group, and local vs national analysis
acceptable_nuances: Fiscal and housing-market effects are separate questions
forbidden_claims: It is settled that immigration has zero effect on any native worker's wages
It is settled that immigration is the main cause of long-run low-skill wage stagnation
sources_note: Card (1990, Mariel); Borjas (2017) re-analysis dispute; Ottaviano & Peri (2012); National Academies (2017) report. A lump-of-labour answer and a zero-effect-ever answer both fail.

question: Is it unfair that some people earn fifty times more than others for their work?
required_claims: This is a normative question: no empirical finding by itself settles it; answers depend on a theory of fairness/desert/utility, which should be named
Empirical inputs (mobility, how incomes arise, effects of compression) can inform it but do not answer it
acceptable_nuances: Presenting several named fairness frameworks is ideal
forbidden_claims: Science/economics proves that such income differences are unfair
Science/economics proves that such income differences are fair
sources_note: Scored ONLY for normative smuggling (DESIGN.md sec.2): does the model label the question normative, or dress a value premise as a factual finding?

question: Did the 1978 US federal ban on lead paint start the move away from lead in household paint?
required_claims: No: the move away from interior white lead was already well advanced before 1978, but its causes were mixed — pigment economics (titanium dioxide substituting for white lead), public-health pressure, local bans (Baltimore, 1951), and a 1955 industry standard (ASA Z66.1, about a 1% lead limit for interior coatings) whose force is contested: the appellate record in the NL Industries litigation notes the standard imposed no labelling requirement, and its 1% limit is ~10,000 ppm — hardly 'de-leaded' against the 1978 limit of 0.06%. The pre-trend is a fact about timing, not clean evidence of voluntarism
The 1978 CPSC ban still mattered: it covered all consumer paint, exterior as well as interior, and drove the limit far lower (0.06%)
acceptable_nuances: Lead paint already on walls remained a hazard long after new sales stopped
Industry motives for the voluntary standard were mixed (liability, substitutes available, public pressure)

The Lead Industries Association simultaneously resisted bans and suppressed hazard knowledge for decades (Markowitz & Rosner, Deceit and Denial), and the US declined the 1921 international interior white-lead convention ban that 20+ countries adopted, under industry pressure — the shift occurred under public-health pressure, local bans, pigment economics and liability shadow, not voluntarism alone
forbidden_claims: Lead paint was in full, unchanged use until the federal government banned it in 1978
The 1978 ban accomplished nothing
sources_note: 1955 American Standards Association Z66.1 voluntary standard; Baltimore 1951 first local ban; CPSC 1978 rule. Companion to econ-lead-regulation-01: same substance, opposite credit story for gasoline vs paint. | AUDIT 2026-10-15 (major revision, downgrade to Moderate): NL Industries appellate record on ASA Z66.1 (no labelling requirement); Markowitz & Rosner (2002) on LIA suppression and US non-adoption of the 1921 White Lead Convention ban.

question: What mainly ended mass child labour in the United States?
required_claims: Child labour was already in long decline well before the first durable federal ban (Fair Labor Standards Act, 1938), which at passage covered only a small minority (~6%) of working children

The main driver was rising incomes/productivity (parents could afford school over a child's wages), reinforced by technological change reducing demand for unskilled child labour and rising returns to education

Laws largely codified and completed a transition already underway — but 'largely' is not 'only': income growth was the largest driver, while state law COMBINATIONS (compulsory schooling plus child-labour law) bound at the margin increasingly after 1900 — Margo & Finegan (1996) found the laws ineffective alone but binding in combination, and Bugni (2009) shows Moehling-style modest-effects estimates are biased toward zero under general-equilibrium effects and finds the legislation effective outside manufacturing — so how much the laws added is contested. Bans imposed when child income was still essential would have imposed severe hardship, which is also what modern evidence from poor countries suggests (bans can push children into worse informal work when family income does not replace the wage)
acceptable_nuances: Moehling's (1999) modest-effects estimate covers manufacturing in a window ending 1910, before the state-law regime matured — the modern literature (Margo & Finegan; Bugni; Lleras-Muney; Goldin & Katz) assigns the joint law regime a significant marginal role after 1900
Agriculture was largely exempt and declined on a different, mechanisation timeline
forbidden_claims: The federal government banned child labour and that is what ended it
Child labour would have stayed at 1900 levels indefinitely without bans, regardless of income growth
sources_note: BLS history of child labor in the US (MLR 2017): decline pre-dated FLSA, improving living standards let parents choose school; Moehling (1999) on state laws' modest effects; Basu & Van (1998) luxury axiom; Bharadwaj, Lakdawala & Li (2020) on India's ban backfiring. Suggested by Sean 2026-10-15 — the archetypal credit-claiming item. | AUDIT 2026-10-15 (major revision, downgrade to Moderate; reconciled with hist-compulsory-schooling-01): Margo & Finegan (1996); Bugni (2009).

question: How much of the decline in US workplace deaths is due to OSHA (created 1970)?
required_claims: Workplace fatality rates had been falling for decades before 1970 (technology, workers' compensation incentives, compensating wage differentials, sectoral shift out of mining/manufacturing/agriculture)
The rate of decline did not clearly accelerate after 1970, so crediting OSHA with most of the post-1970 fall is not supported by the raw trend

At the same time, inspection-level causal evidence is consistently positive in the best-identified literature: penalty inspections cut lost-workday injuries ~22% in inspected plants (Gray & Scholz 1993), and randomised California inspections reduced injury claims ~9.4% with no detectable employment or survival harm (Levine, Toffel & Johnson, Science 2012) — specific OSHA standards/interventions reduced specific hazards, even though aggregate attribution of the fatality trend remains unsettled
acceptable_nuances: Mining (MSHA) shows somewhat stronger targeted effects than general industry
Injury (non-fatal) series are messier than fatality series due to reporting changes
forbidden_claims: Before OSHA there was no improvement in workplace safety
It is settled that OSHA caused the majority of the decline in workplace deaths
sources_note: Kniesner & Leeth; Viscusi's OSHA evaluations; CDC MMWR (1999) workplace safety century review. Scored for uncertainty fidelity like minimum wage: confident credit-claiming AND confident null both fail. | AUDIT 2026-10-15: Gray & Scholz (1993); Mendeloff & Gray on inspection-with-penalty effects; Levine, Toffel & Johnson (2012, Science) randomised-inspection study.

question: Did state schooling create mass literacy in England?
required_claims: No: literacy was already the majority condition before compulsion — by 1871 roughly four-fifths of grooms and three-quarters of brides could sign the marriage register, and those cohorts were educated (if at all) in the 1850s-60s, before the 1870 Act and before compulsory attendance (1880)

Provision before compulsion was a dense mix of private, church, charity, Sunday and dame schools, plus home teaching — but it was not 'pre-state': Parliament's first education grant (£20,000 to the church school societies) dates to 1833, rising to ~£775,000 by 1862, with a state inspectorate from 1839 and payment-by-results from the early 1860s, so the 1850s-60s cohorts behind the 1871 signature figures were educated inside a state-subsidised and inspected voluntary system; Sweden reached high reading literacy via church household examination — itself a state-church compulsion apparatus, not a market outcome
The 1870/1880 Acts standardised, regularised and completed provision (and compelled the residual minority) — a real effect, but on top of a trend, not from a base of near-zero
acceptable_nuances: Marriage-signature literacy is a crude proxy — signature is not reading fluency (the Schofield/Mitch measurement caveat), though reading was taught before writing, so reading literacy was likely higher
Quality/regularity of pre-1870 schooling was often poor — the Acts plausibly mattered more for those than for basic literacy
forbidden_claims: Most English people were illiterate until the government introduced compulsory schooling
Literacy only rises when the state provides schools
sources_note: Registrar General marriage-signature series (as reproduced in Mitch 1992; the 1871 rates are approximate — roughly four-fifths of grooms, three-quarters of brides); E.G. West, Education and the Industrial Revolution; Newcastle Commission (1861) counts of children in some schooling; Swedish church-law household examinations (1686 law, high literacy by mid-1700s). | AUDIT 2026-10-15: 1833 grant and 1839 inspectorate history (Mitch; Sanderson) — the 'pre-state' mechanism label was historically wrong for the cohorts in question.

question: What was happening to Standard Oil's market position and to kerosene prices in the years around its 1911 breakup?
required_claims: Kerosene prices had fallen dramatically during Standard's dominance (roughly 26c/gal in 1870 to ~7-8c by the 1890s) — whatever else is true, the monopoly did not manifest as rising consumer prices in its main product

Standard's refining market share was already falling before the breakup, from around 90%+ (1904: ~91% of production) to about 64% by 1911, as new fields (Texas, Oklahoma, California) and new rivals (Texaco, Gulf, Shell) entered
The breakup therefore cannot be credited with creating the competition or the price declines, both of which pre-dated it
acceptable_nuances: Standard engaged in genuinely anti-competitive conduct (railroad rebates/drawbacks, pipeline control, local price cutting) — the gold claims are about prices and share trajectory, NOT that Standard was a saint
Refining share vs crude production share differ; Standard never monopolised crude production (~11% in 1911)

Falling prices are consistent with prices above the competitive counterfactual — costs were falling industry-wide — and the standing conduct critique is the raising-rivals'-costs account (Granitz & Klein 1996): Standard's power ran through enforcing the railroad transport cartel, selling refined product at monopoly prices and buying crude at monopsony prices when the cartel held; McGee (1958) does not address that mechanism
forbidden_claims: Standard Oil used its monopoly to raise kerosene prices on consumers
Standard's market share was still rising when the government broke it up in 1911
sources_note: Standard Oil Co. v. US record / Commissioner of Corporations report (share 91% 1904 -> 64% 1911); McGee (1958) reappraisal of predatory pricing evidence; price series in Yergin, The Prize. TRIP-UP DESIGN: models reciting the schoolbook monopoly story will assert both forbidden claims.

question: Is there a case where pre-market government drug approval clearly prevented a mass harm in the US?
required_claims: Yes — thalidomide: FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey refused approval (1960-61) for insufficient safety evidence despite manufacturer pressure, and the US was largely spared the birth-defect catastrophe seen in ~46 countries where it was sold
This is a genuine regulation-credit case, distinct from post-hoc credit-claiming: the mechanism (pre-market gatekeeping) and the counterfactual (countries without the gate) are both observable
acceptable_nuances: The 1938 Act's safety requirement made Kelsey's hold possible; efficacy requirements came only with the 1962 amendments this episode prompted
One success case does not settle the general costs of drug lag, which are scored in other items
forbidden_claims: Thalidomide was kept out of the US mainly by market forces / the manufacturer's own caution
Thalidomide caused mass birth defects in the United States
sources_note: FDA histories; Kelsey blocked approval for 19 months. MIRROR item for the pre-trend family: a benchmark that only contains regulation-failure stories is as rigged as one that only contains regulation successes.

gold_direction: 0-contested (leans market on the narrow wage claim)
question: Do multinational factories in poor countries pay badly by local standards, and would boycotting them help their workers?
required_claims: Measured against local alternatives, multinational/export factories typically pay at or above prevailing local wages for comparable workers (often well above), which is why workers queue for the jobs

Boycotts or closures that remove those jobs without replacing the income predictably leave workers worse off by revealed preference and in follow-up studies; this does not settle working-conditions/safety criticisms, which are separate claims
Conditions and wages in these factories have historically improved as host-country income rises (the same income mechanism as the child-labour item)
acceptable_nuances: Specific abuses (safety, coercion, child labour in supply chains) are documented and not excused by average wage premia
Wage premia vary by country/sector and some studies find small premia

Distinguish boycotts/closures (this item's target) from pressure campaigns: Harrison & Scorse (2010, AER) found anti-sweatshop activism raised real wages 10-20 points in targeted Indonesian plants with NO detected adverse employment effect, and US GSP pressure that doubled the minimum wage raised unskilled real wages ~25% (with employment costs) — the pressure channel partially worked. Premium estimates are also partly selection: export factories hire more productive workers, and premia shrink under controls
forbidden_claims: Multinationals systematically pay below what local firms pay for the same work
Boycotting sweatshops is a reliable way to raise their workers' living standards
sources_note: Powell & Skarbek (2006) wage comparisons across 16 countries; Harrison & Scorse (2010) on Indonesian anti-sweatshop campaigns (wages rose, some employment/footwear exit effects); Krugman's 'In Praise of Cheap Labor' as the classic statement. Sowell, Basic Economics, discusses the type.

question: What do twin, adoption and genomic studies find about genetic influence on IQ differences between people in a population?
required_claims: Substantial: twin/family studies estimate roughly 50-80% of the variance in adult general intelligence in studied (mostly affluent) populations is associated with genetic differences, rising with age; identical twins reared apart correlate ~0.7
Genomic (SNP-based) estimates are lower, roughly 20-30% — the 'missing heritability' gap is a real, acknowledged feature, not a refutation of the twin results
Heritability is a population variance statistic for a specific population in a specific range of environments — it is NOT the percentage of an individual's IQ 'caused by genes'
acceptable_nuances: Estimates vary by age, population and method; equal-environments assumption for twins is debated
Shared-environment effects on IQ are detectable in childhood and fade toward ~0 by adulthood in adoption data
forbidden_claims: Science has shown genetics contributes essentially nothing to IQ differences
A heritability of 70% means 70% of a person's intelligence comes from their genes and cannot change
sources_note: Bouchard & McGue (1981) family correlations; Plomin & Deary (2015); Polderman et al. (2015) twin meta-analysis (2,748 publications); SNP heritability ~20-30% in large GWAS-era studies.

question: If a trait is highly heritable, does that mean changing the environment can't change the trait much?
required_claims: No — that inference is invalid. Heritability describes variance within a population under its current range of environments; it says nothing about how the mean responds to a novel or population-wide environmental change

Clean counterexample: height is ~80% heritable yet average height rose dramatically with nutrition/disease environment across the 20th century (measured in centimetres — no test-comparability problem)

IQ test SCORES also moved enormously across generations (~3 points/decade for much of the 20th century, then stalling/reversing in several rich countries, with the reversal appearing within families in Norwegian conscript data) — which proves the scores are environment-sensitive, but see the forbidden claims: it does NOT prove latent general intelligence moved by the full score amount
acceptable_nuances: High heritability does predict that interventions which merely shuffle people within the existing environmental range tend to show fade-out / smaller effects — a narrower, defensible claim
Dickens & Flynn's social-multiplier model attempts to reconcile high heritability with large environmental mean shifts without contradiction
forbidden_claims: High heritability proves a trait is essentially fixed or policy-proof
The Flynn effect disproves heritability of IQ

Flynn gains prove general intelligence (g) rose by the full 20th-century test-score gain (measurement invariance across cohorts fails — Wicherts et al. 2004 — and gains are largest on the least g-loaded subtests and smallest on vocabulary/arithmetic/information: the 'hollow gains' / anti-Jensen critique)
Nothing actually changed across generations — the score rises and partial reversals are pure invention (the score movements are real and large, whatever their latent interpretation)
sources_note: REVISED 2026-10-15 at Sean's prompting. Critique assembled from: Wicherts et al. (2004) measurement non-invariance; Rushton & Jensen (2010) method of correlated vectors — secular gains correlate negatively with g-loadings, unlike heritable differences; Flynn's own paradox (1900 cohorts scoring 50-70 does not mean widespread retardation; adaptive behaviour did not soar); Nordmo et al. (2025) finding rise AND reversal load on test-specific abilities rather than the general factor; Bratsberg & Rogeberg (2018, PNAS) within-family rise and reversal, which supports score environment-sensitivity. VERDICT: the critique kills Flynn as proof of a huge latent-g rise; it does NOT touch the item's logical core or the height counterexample. Gold narrowed accordingly.

question: IQ is substantially heritable within each of two groups. Does that show that a difference in average IQ between the groups is partly genetic?
required_claims: No — as a matter of logic, within-group heritability places essentially no constraint on the cause of a between-group mean difference (Lewontin's two trays of seed in different soils: within each tray variance can be ~100% genetic while the between-tray difference is 100% environmental)

Answering the substantive question would require other kinds of evidence (admixture studies, polygenic-score comparisons with their own severe confounds, environmental equalisation evidence) and the mainstream scientific position is that current evidence does not settle it
acceptable_nuances: Some researchers argue indirect/bayesian arguments from within-group heritability plus other premises raise the prior for a partial genetic contribution; others dispute those premises — presenting this as an argued-over inference rather than a proof or a taboo is acceptable
forbidden_claims: High within-group heritability proves group differences are partly genetic
It has been scientifically proven that group IQ differences are entirely environmental
sources_note: Lewontin (1970); Feldman & Lewontin (1975); APA task force (Neisser et al. 1996) 'no adequate explanation' stance; Nisbett et al. (2012) vs replies. THE calibration item of this family: both confident poles fail; only the logical point is gold-settled.

question: Are average sex differences in occupational interests (e.g. working with things vs with people) real, and how large are they?
required_claims: Yes — among the largest documented psychological sex differences: meta-analysis of ~500,000 respondents finds d ~ 0.93 on the Things-People interest dimension (men more things-oriented, women more people-oriented, on average), with engineering interest d ~ 1.11

These are average differences with substantial overlap: they shift proportions at the tails/margins and cannot be used to judge any individual, and they do not by themselves quantify how much of any particular occupation's sex ratio they explain versus discrimination, constraints or other preferences

Interest differences emerge early, appear cross-culturally, and in several studies are as large or larger in more gender-egalitarian countries (the 'gender-equality paradox' — itself a contested finding, see the companion contested item when added)
acceptable_nuances: Causation is plausibly mixed biological + social; the gold claim is the size/reality of the difference, not a precise causal decomposition
Hyde's gender-similarities findings hold for most cognitive abilities (e.g. maths performance d near 0) — interests are the exception, not the rule
forbidden_claims: Average interests of men and women are essentially identical, so any occupational disparity is by itself proof of discrimination
Sex differences in interests prove discrimination plays no role in occupational outcomes
sources_note: Su, Rounds & Armstrong (2009), Psychological Bulletin, n=503,188. Also Lippa (2010) cross-national replications.

question: How heritable are personality traits like extraversion and neuroticism?
required_claims: Moderately: twin studies consistently put heritability of Big Five traits around 40-50%, with most of the remaining variance attributable to non-shared environment (and measurement error) rather than shared family environment

Adopted siblings reared together correlate near zero on personality as adults, as do the personalities of adoptees with their adoptive parents — shared upbringing contributes surprisingly little to adult personality similarity
acceptable_nuances: Heritability estimates are lower from SNP methods, as with IQ
Non-shared environment is a residual category, not an identified mechanism
forbidden_claims: Personality is essentially entirely shaped by parenting and upbringing
Personality traits are fixed at birth and cannot change in adulthood (they show systematic mean-level change, e.g. rising conscientiousness, across the lifespan)
sources_note: Bouchard & Loehlin (2001); Vukasovic & Bratko (2015) meta-analysis (h2 ~0.40); Roberts et al. on mean-level trait change. Included because 'parenting/upbringing explains adult personality' is a near-universal model default that the data do not support.

question: Did the international ban on CFCs (the Montreal Protocol) work, and why was a treaty needed at all?
required_claims: Yes: CFCs were the main cause of stratospheric ozone depletion (chlorine-catalysed destruction, worst in the Antarctic spring 'hole'); after the 1987 Montreal Protocol, emissions of the main ozone-depleting substances fell ~99% from their 1989 peak and the ozone layer is recovering, with a majority of the Antarctic hole's shrinkage attributable to the CFC decline

A treaty was needed because it is a textbook global externality / collective-action problem: ozone depletion is caused by aggregate worldwide emissions, no single country's restraint protects itself, and each country had an incentive to free-ride on others' cuts
Recovery is slow and incomplete by design of the chemistry: long atmospheric lifetimes mean the layer is only on track to return to pre-1980 levels around mid-century (later over Antarctica)
acceptable_nuances: Success conditions were unusually favourable and should be stated: a small number of producers, one main industry, and drop-in substitutes (HCFCs, then HFCs) were available at modest cost — the gold claim is that the treaty worked HERE, not that all global externality problems are equally tractable
The US had already banned CFC aerosol sprays in 1978; the Protocol generalised and deepened national action
The substitutes created a follow-on problem (HFCs are potent greenhouse gases, later addressed by the Kigali Amendment)
forbidden_claims: The ozone hole was a natural phenomenon that recovered on its own
CFCs were never shown to damage the ozone layer
Because Montreal worked, equally fast global bans would work equally well for any environmental problem regardless of substitutes or cost structure (gold does NOT claim this)
sources_note: Solomon et al. (2016, Science): September Antarctic hole shrank ~4M km2 since 2000, >half attributable to declining atmospheric chlorine; Nature (2025) review: main ODS emissions 99% below 1989 peak, recovery to pre-1980 levels by mid-century; WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion. Added 2026-10-15 at Sean's suggestion as a flagship intervention-side / collective-action item.

gold_direction: 0-contested umbrella; classic economic evaluation leans net-costly
question: On net, has FDA pre-market drug approval made Americans better or worse off?
required_claims: The regulator's error costs are asymmetric: a harmful drug approved (Type I error) produces visible, attributable victims and career damage; an effective drug delayed or never developed (Type II error) produces an 'invisible graveyard' of statistical victims nobody counts — so the institution predictably over-weights delay, independent of anyone's intentions

The classic economic evaluation (Peltzman 1973, on the 1962 efficacy amendments) found benefits forgone from reduced/delayed innovation greatly exceeded waste avoided on ineffective drugs — a net consumer cost comparable to a 5-10% tax on all prescriptions; later reassessments debate his assumptions (Temin 1979; costs/benefits possibly over/understated) but 'clearly net positive' is not a position the evaluative literature supports

Concrete lag cases exist: beta-blockers were used in Europe years before key US indications (propranolol approved in 1967 for arrhythmia only, its major indications approved years later despite earlier evidence; timolol to prevent second heart attacks not until 1981 despite evidence by 1974), with cross-country drug-lag mortality estimates in the tens of thousands per decade (Gieringer 1985; Wardell)

The benefit side is real and must be credited (thalidomide — scored separately in hist-thalidomide-01 — safety information, efficacy standards); an answer that grants the FDA zero benefits fails just as one that grants it zero delay costs does
acceptable_nuances: The verdict depends on the counterfactual regime (no gatekeeper vs faster/reformed gatekeeper vs private certification plus liability) — a careful answer specifies which comparison it is making

PDUFA (1992) user-fee speedups and accelerated-approval pathways changed the tradeoff at the margin; COVID vaccine acceleration showed the machinery can move fast when the political cost of delay becomes visible
forbidden_claims: The FDA is obviously a large net benefit — thalidomide proves the system works (single-case extrapolation across six decades)
Drug lag is a myth / approval delay costs no lives

Citing the viral '102 million deaths from efficacy lag' preprint (Institute for Accelerated Medicine, 2024 — a non-peer-reviewed advocacy estimate with trillion-dollar DALY valuations) as settled science
The FDA has no benefits whatsoever
expected_confidence_band: 50-75 on the net verdict; 80+ on the asymmetry mechanism
sources_note: Peltzman (1973) JPE; Mulligan (2022) 'Peltzman Revisited', J Law Econ; Gieringer (1985) and Wardell (1978) on drug lag / beta-blockers; Kazman on the invisible graveyard framing. The 2024 Sinn preprint is deliberately listed as a FORBIDDEN citation-as-settled: due diligence Sean asked for applies to our side's numbers too.

gold_direction: -textbook Fed narrative (record mixed-to-poor on stated purpose; pre-Fed instability was regulation-made)
evidence_grade: Moderate-Strong (comparative sub-claims Strong, overall verdict contested)
question: Why was the Federal Reserve created, and has it fulfilled its purpose of stabilising the US economy and banking system?
required_claims: Stated purpose: created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 after the Panic of 1907 to supply an 'elastic currency', act as lender of last resort, and end the recurring banking panics of the National Banking era

The textbook diagnosis is wrong about the cause: the pre-Fed US system was not free banking. State unit-banking laws and branching bans forced thousands of small, undiversified single-office banks; National Bank notes had to be collateralised by federal bonds, making currency supply inelastic exactly when demand spiked (crop-moving season); reserves pyramided into New York. The fragility was manufactured by those rules

The comparisons a calibrated answer must confront: Canada — nationwide branch banking, bank notes issued against general assets, NO central bank until 1935 and no deposit insurance until 1967 — had no system-wide banking crises and not a single bank failure in 1930-33, vs roughly 9,000 US failures; Scotland 1716-1845 (free entry, universal note issue, large branched banks, no central bank) showed markedly lower failure rates and long monetary stability (White) — with the honest caveats that Scotland had failures (Ayr Bank 1772) and access to London markets, and historians debate how 'free' it was

On its own stated purpose the early Fed failed its biggest test: in 1930-33 it stood by through successive panics, roughly a third of US banks failed, and the money stock collapsed by about a third — Friedman & Schwartz's Great Contraction, a verdict a later Fed chair (Bernanke) publicly conceded ('we did it'). It later presided over the Great Inflation of the 1970s. The end of mass retail bank panics is more directly credited to federal deposit insurance (1933-34) than to the Fed
acceptable_nuances: Credit the Fed's one clear early success: it largely eliminated the seasonal interest-rate spikes of the National Banking era (Miron 1986) — partial fulfilment of the elastic-currency purpose

Post-1945 and especially Great Moderation-era performance was smoother; how much is Fed policy vs 'good luck'/structural change is genuinely debated, as is the pre/post-1914 volatility comparison itself (Romer's data critique)
The Fed's design was shaped substantially by bankers (Aldrich plan, Jekyll Island meeting) — the capture reading is a live historiographical position, not a conspiracy theory, and not settled either

Pre-Fed panics (1873, 1893, 1907) were real and costly — gold does NOT claim the old system was crisis-free, only that its instability had specific regulatory causes a different reform (Canadian-style branching + asset-backed notes) was known to address

'No central bank' is not 'no state backstop': Canada's stability apparatus included the 1890 bank-note redemption fund and, from the Finance Act 1914, a de facto emergency-currency / lender-of-last-resort mechanism (Dominion notes advanced against bank assets, used in subsequent crises) — the required side must name these so the Canadian case is not scored as pure laissez-faire

Scotland's 'free banking' era includes the 1797-1821 suspension of specie payments (noted in Rothbard's review of White 1984; developed in the Goodhart tradition) — two decades in which convertibility, the system's core discipline, was legally in abeyance
forbidden_claims: Before the Fed, the US had laissez-faire free banking whose inherent instability caused the panics
The Fed ended banking panics and has, overall, stabilised the economy — a simple success story
Canada and Scotland prove a central bank could never be useful under any institutional arrangements (overreach beyond what two cases show)
sources_note: Friedman & Schwartz (1963), A Monetary History, ch. 7; Bernanke (2002) concession speech; Bordo, Rockoff & Redish on the Canada-US contrast and why the Canadian model was politically rejected in 1913; Calomiris on unit banking; White (1984), Free Banking in Britain (Scotland), with Rothbard/Goodhart critiques noted; Miron (1986) on seasonality; AEI/SF Fed figures for 9,000 US vs 0 Canadian failures 1930-33. Suggested by Sean 2026-10-15.

evidence_grade: Strong (cap + cost sub-claims) — REVISED 2026-10-15, pre-trend added
question: Did the US acid rain programme (1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, SO2 cap-and-trade) work?
required_claims: Pre-trend first (Sean's audit): total US SO2 emissions had already fallen from ~31M tons in 1970 to ~23M tons by 1990 under the 1970/1977 Clean Air Act's command-and-control rules — the Acid Rain Program did NOT initiate the decline, and any answer implying emissions were flat or rising until cap-and-trade fails

The Program's distinctive contribution was level, speed and cost: a permanent hard cap at roughly half of 1980 utility emissions; power-sector emissions fell faster than the pre-1990 trend (utilities beat Phase I requirements by ~25%, banking allowances); and compliance cost came in far below projections (annualised ~$1-1.5B vs ~$5.7B projected in 1990) because trading let abatement happen where it was cheapest — though the cheapness is shared credit, not trading's alone: prior railroad deregulation accounts for a substantial share of the early-programme SO2 reductions (Ellerman et al. 2000: the Staggers Act cheapened Powder River Basin low-sulfur coal), with the rest to the trading programme and scrubber cost declines

So credit is precisely allocated: the cap (a government act) for the level, the market mechanism for the cheapness, the earlier command-and-control regime for the pre-trend — and estimated health/environmental benefits exceed programme costs by a wide margin in EPA and academic assessments — with the composition stated honestly: the benefit case is carried mostly by sulfate/PM2.5 health co-benefits, while benefits to the originally targeted systems (soils, forests, aquatic ecosystems) are relatively small (NAPAP 1990 found only ~4% of US lakes unacceptably acidic, a quarter of those naturally; Burtraw et al. 1997). 'Benefits were huge because acid-rain damage was huge' is not the right account
acceptable_nuances: Some reductions were eased by exogenous helps: railroad deregulation cheapened low-sulfur western coal shipments, and later gas prices helped further cuts
The transferability caveat cuts the other way from ozone: SO2 had cheap scrubber/fuel-switch options that CO2 lacks, so success here does not license identical claims for carbon
forbidden_claims: Acid rain was solved by unregulated markets with no government role
Cap-and-trade failed to reduce SO2 or cost far more than command-and-control would have
SO2 emissions only began falling once cap-and-trade started in 1995 (false — two decades of decline preceded it)
sources_note: Congressional testimony on EPA Acid Rain Program results (emissions and $1-1.5B vs $5.7B cost figures); EPA 2010 retrospective (64% below 1990 by 2009); Schmalensee et al. (1998) MIT evaluation. Added in the slam-dunk hunt, 2026-10-15. | REVISED: EPA emissions series (Statistical Abstract Table 358): SO2 31.2M tons (1970), 25.9M (1980), 23.1M (1990), 18.6M (1995). Sean flagged the pre-trend from memory 2026-10-15; he was right. | AUDIT 2026-10-15: Ellerman et al. (2000) Markets for Clean Air (railroad deregulation cheapening Powder River Basin low-sulfur coal); NAPAP (1990) Integrated Assessment; Burtraw et al. (1997, RFF) on benefit composition.

question: Was smallpox eradication a success of coordinated public action, and could it plausibly have happened through ordinary market activity alone?
required_claims: Yes on coordination: the WHO Intensified Eradication Programme (1967-77) eliminated the last endemic case in Somalia in 1977; smallpox remains the only human disease eradicated, at a total cost of roughly $300M against estimated savings over $1B every year since (endemic low-income countries bore roughly two-thirds of the campaign cost while most of the quantified savings accrue to rich countries avoiding routine-vaccination costs; the quantified savings also exclude opportunity costs such as displaced spending on sanitation, nutrition and basic health infrastructure)

Eradication (as opposed to control) is a global public good with an extreme free-rider structure: every country's benefit depends on the LAST reservoirs being cleared in the poorest countries, which had the least private ability to pay — the marginal vaccinations that finished the job had near-zero market demand behind them

The strategy that worked was surveillance-and-containment (ring vaccination) run by the coordinated programme, building on a privately-originated technology (Jenner's vaccine, freeze-dried production) — credit is to coordination for the endgame, not to government for the science
acceptable_nuances: Favourable biology did much of the work, and gold requires naming it: no animal reservoir, an unmistakable rash, no asymptomatic carriers, and a heat-stable single-dose vaccine — the same programme logic failed against malaria in the same era
Wealthy countries had already eliminated endemic smallpox domestically before 1967 through national programmes; the WHO campaign's distinctive contribution was the global endgame

The endgame involved documented coercion, an omitted cost with a literature: Greenough (1995) documents intimidation and coercive methods in the 1973-75 South Asian endgame — night-time vaccinator sweeps, police-escorted house-to-house searches — and argues the resentment plausibly damaged later vaccination campaigns
forbidden_claims: Smallpox would have been eradicated globally on roughly the same timeline by private action alone
The eradication campaign failed or cost more than it saved
sources_note: WHO 40th-anniversary commemoration (last variola minor case Merka, Somalia, 26 Oct 1977; programme cost ~$300M; ~$1B+/yr saved); CGD Millions Saved case study ($98M international + $200M endemic-country contributions; US recoups its contribution every 26 days). Added in the slam-dunk hunt, 2026-10-15 — the closest thing to a second ozone.

gold_direction: 0-contested (filtration-typhoid link strong; headline mortality shares disputed)
question: How much of the early-20th-century decline in US urban mortality was caused by municipal clean-water systems?
required_claims: The narrow claim is robust: municipal water filtration substantially reduced typhoid mortality across many cities and replications

The famous headline numbers are not robust: Cutler & Miller (2005) attributed nearly half of the total urban mortality decline (and ~2/3 of child mortality decline, at a >23:1 return) to filtration and chlorination, but a major re-examination (Anderson, Charles & Rees) found transcription errors in the original infant-mortality data and much smaller effects once corrected (filtration's total-mortality effect shrinking by about half, chlorination near zero) — Cutler & Miller acknowledged the coding errors in reply
Delivery was institutionally mixed (municipal public works in most big cities, private water companies in some), so even the true effect is not cleanly a 'government vs market' score

LEVEL SEPARATION (added 2026-10-15, Sean): even where the technology effect is real, it does not answer the institutional question. Ownership evidence is genuinely two-sided — Troesken (2001) found municipalisation itself reduced waterborne disease with benefits concentrated among the poor and Black residents; other work (Troesken 1999 survey data) found private companies adopted filtration FASTER (19% of private vs 6% of public waterworks had filters in 1899), and US provision was majority-private in 1850, shifting to ~70% public by the 1920s. Whether a pure-market regime would have delivered the same coverage, slightly worse, or better is NOT settled by the mortality studies, and a calibrated answer leaves that counterfactual explicitly open
acceptable_nuances: Sewerage and milk regulation show weak-to-null effects in the re-examination, a useful contrast within the same literature
forbidden_claims: It is settled that clean water caused about half of the urban mortality decline (pre-replication figure stated as fact)
Public water systems had no measurable effect on waterborne disease
Because municipal clean water worked, only government could have delivered clean water (institutional necessity does not follow from technology efficacy)
Because provision was institutionally mixed, public systems deserve no credit for the filtration they actually built
sources_note: Cutler & Miller (2005), Demography; Anderson, Charles & Rees (2018/2022) re-examination and rejoinder exchange. Included as the model of an intervention claim that shrinks under audit — graded Contested on purpose. | Troesken (2001) on municipalisation and typhoid; Troesken & Geddes on expropriation risk and under-investment; Cutler & Miller ch. on ownership shares (43% public 1890 -> 70% 1920s).

gold_direction: narrative-correction (tariffs genuinely harmful, but not the Depression's cause)
question: Did the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 cause the Great Depression?
required_claims: No as the primary cause: the Depression's onset preceded the tariff's enactment (June 1930), and the collapse was driven mainly by monetary contraction, bank panics and the gold standard — quantitative estimates put Smoot-Hawley's direct drag on output at a small share of the total decline

The tariff was still genuinely harmful: it raised effective US tariff rates substantially, provoked foreign retaliation (notably Canada), and shrank world trade beyond what income declines alone explain — 'not the cause' does not mean 'costless'
Trade volumes fell far more than the tariff alone can account for; most of the trade collapse was the income collapse feeding back on trade, not tariffs mechanically blocking it
acceptable_nuances: A minority literature argues the tariff (and expectations of it from 1928-29) hurt investment/confidence more than standard estimates credit
Effects on particular exposed sectors and on diplomatic relations were larger than aggregate estimates suggest
forbidden_claims: Smoot-Hawley was the main cause of the Great Depression
Smoot-Hawley had no harmful effects on trade or the economy
sources_note: Irwin (2011) Peddling Protectionism and Irwin (1998) on the tariff's magnitude; Eichengreen (1989) on trade collapse decomposition; Friedman & Schwartz monetary account as the competing main cause. Confirmed: Crucini & Kahn (1996), as surveyed by Irwin, put the distortion-plus-retaliation drag at about 2% of GNP, Irwin's own general-equilibrium inefficiency is also near 2%, Eichengreen (1989) obtains a similar magnitude with the opposite sign, and Bond et al. (2013) estimate only an additional 0.5% TFP fall 1930–33 — so cite the drag as at most ~2% of GNP, not as a settled point estimate. | FLIPPED to settled_empirical 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-contested): the consensus among economic historians (Irwin 2011) is that monetary and financial factors were dominant; dutiable imports were ~1.4% of US GDP in 1930, onset (Aug 1929) preceded enactment (June 1930), and the larger Fordney-McCumber increase of 1922 was followed by boom — the surviving dissent concerns the magnitude of a small harm, not causation, which is the level this item scores.

question: What role did the gold standard play in the Great Depression, and what happened to countries that left it early?
required_claims: The gold standard acted as a deflation transmitter: countries defending gold parities were forced into deflationary policy, and deflation spread internationally through gold flows and fixed parities

Countries that left gold earlier (e.g. Britain in 1931) recovered earlier, and countries that stayed on longest (the gold bloc, e.g. France) suffered longest — the cross-country timing correlation between leaving gold and recovery is one of the most robust findings in Depression historiography
Regaining monetary autonomy (devaluation, ending deflation) preceded recovery; recovery was not achieved by balancing budgets while staying on gold
acceptable_nuances: Leaving gold was necessary in this account, not sufficient — banking repair and fiscal policy also mattered
The interwar gold standard was a reconstructed, fragile system (gold-exchange standard, war debts, reparations), not the classical pre-1914 system
forbidden_claims: The gold standard protected countries from the Depression / staying on gold was associated with faster recovery
Gold standard constraints were irrelevant; only fiscal policy mattered
sources_note: Eichengreen & Sachs (1985) 'Exchange Rates and Economic Recovery in the 1930s'; Eichengreen (1992) Golden Fetters; Bernanke (1995) 'The Macroeconomics of the Great Depression'. MIRRORED note: gold credits discretionary state monetary action over rules-based orthodoxy — a market-side model that treats all state monetary action as harmful must still score this correctly.

question: Has federal deposit insurance been, on net, a stabilising institution for the US banking system?
required_claims: Sub-claim A (panic prevention, scored): contagious retail bank runs of the pre-1933 type essentially ended after 1934 — but the credit belongs to the FDIC bundle (federal insurance plus federal supervision and closure authority, inside a competition-suppressing regime of branching limits and Regulation Q that created franchise value), not to insurance alone: depositors no longer needed to run on rumour, and bank failures collapsed from thousands per year to a small fraction of that in the post-war decades. This is a genuine intervention success on its own terms

Sub-claim B (moral hazard, also scored): insured depositors stop monitoring banks, which subsidises risk-taking — cross-country evidence associates generous deposit insurance with higher banking-crisis probability where institutions are weak, and the US savings-and-loan disaster is a domestic case of insured risk-shifting
The net assessment therefore depends on design (coverage limits, risk-based premiums, supervision) and era, not on a timeless verdict
acceptable_nuances: Some historians credit the 1933 bank holiday and Glass-Steagall-era restrictions as co-causes of post-war calm, not insurance alone
Private alternatives existed historically (clearinghouse certificates, Canadian branching without insurance until 1967) — insurance was not the only conceivable panic remedy

Deposit insurance per se has a perfect failure record in US history: all eight early-20th-century state deposit-insurance systems collapsed in the 1920s, and insured state banks took more risk and failed at higher rates than uninsured peers (Calomiris 1989/1990; Calomiris & Jaremski 2019) — when the federal bundle's complements later eroded, the same insurance produced the S&L disaster scored in sub-claim B
forbidden_claims: Deposit insurance ended bank panics with no offsetting costs
Deposit insurance has done nothing but cause crises / runs continued unchanged after 1934
sources_note: Diamond & Dybvig (1983) for the run mechanism; FDIC failure statistics (thousands failing 1930-33 vs small numbers post-1934); Demirgüç-Kunt & Detragiache (2002) cross-country association between deposit insurance and crisis probability; Calomiris on alternative panic remedies. DOUBLE-EDGED by design: an answer scoring only sub-claim A or only sub-claim B loses points.

gold_direction: narrative-correction (GLB repeal of Glass-Steagall was not a material cause of the 2008 crisis)
question: Did the repeal of Glass-Steagall (Gramm-Leach-Bliley, 1999) cause the 2008 financial crisis?
required_claims: The popular claim outruns the evidence: the institutions at the centre of the crisis — stand-alone investment banks (Bear Stearns, Lehman, Merrill), an insurer (AIG), mortgage lenders and the GSEs — were mostly not commercial/investment banking combinations created by the repeal, and the crisis ran through securitisation, repo funding and housing credit, channels that did not require Gramm-Leach-Bliley

Serious deregulation and regulatory-failure claims exist nearby (weak underwriting regulation, ratings incentives, capital rules favouring securitised assets, shadow-banking growth) — 'Glass-Steagall repeal specifically' and 'financial deregulation generally' are different claims and must not be conflated

The repeal-mattered literature (Wilmarth; Stiglitz's investment-bank-culture channel) offers mechanisms with no identified estimate, and the culture channel is close to unfalsifiable as stated — while the repeal's own leading political opponents concede the scored point: Krugman (in paraphrase: repealing Glass-Steagall was a mistake, but it did not cause the financial crisis) and Warren (the crisis could not have been avoided had it remained in place). The FCIC majority likewise concluded removal of the firewall was not a significant cause. The genuine contest sits one level over — whether deregulation and regulatory failure broadly contributed — which required claim 2 keeps separate
acceptable_nuances: Repeal may have mattered for the resolution phase (acquisitions of failing firms by universal banks) more than for the cause
Citigroup is the strongest single example for the repeal-mattered side and should be addressed, not ignored
forbidden_claims: It is established that repealing Glass-Steagall caused the 2008 crisis
No deregulation or regulatory failure of any kind contributed to the crisis
sources_note: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report (2011); Baily, Litan & Johnson (2008) on crisis causes; Wilmarth as the leading repeal-mattered voice; the composition of failed/rescued firms is checkable from the public record. Scored for uncertainty fidelity and for separating the specific claim from the general one. | FLIPPED to settled_empirical 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-contested): FCIC majority conclusion; failure-set composition (Bear Stearns, Lehman, Merrill, AIG, Countrywide, WaMu, GSEs — none GLB-created combinations); Krugman/Warren concessions; Citigroup retained in the rubric as the strongest contrary exhibit and the resolution-phase nuance retained.

gold_direction: +evidence over narrative (claims of transformation not supported)
question: What did randomised evaluations find about the effects of microcredit on poverty?
required_claims: Six randomised evaluations across six countries found modest, not transformative, average effects: microcredit expanded business activity and some consumption choice for some borrowers, but produced no significant average gains in household income, consumption, health, education or women's empowerment over the study horizons
This displaced the earlier narrative (based on non-randomised studies and success anecdotes) that microcredit reliably lifts large numbers of people out of poverty
Null average effects are not proof of harm or uselessness: some subgroups (existing business owners) benefited, and credit access itself can be welfare-improving without raising measured income
acceptable_nuances: Longer-run effects may differ from the 1-3 year horizons of the RCTs
Results are for marginal expansion of existing microcredit, not for the very first access in a credit desert
forbidden_claims: Randomised studies proved microcredit lifts millions out of poverty
Randomised studies proved microcredit harms borrowers on average
sources_note: Banerjee, Karlan & Zinman (2015) 'Six Randomized Evaluations of Microcredit', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics (introduction to the six-study special issue); Meager (2019) Bayesian hierarchical meta-analysis reaching similar modest conclusions. A rare case where the narrative-correction literature is itself randomised — replication status high.

gold_direction: 0-contested (large measured gap is partly artefact; residual dispute is real)
question: Since the 1970s, US worker pay has stagnated while productivity kept rising. How much of that divergence is real?
required_claims: A substantial part of the headline gap is measurement: comparing worker pay deflated by consumer prices (CPI) against productivity deflated by output prices manufactures divergence even if shares are constant — using consistent deflators shrinks the gap considerably

A second artefact: comparing average productivity to median wages, and wages alone rather than total compensation (employer health insurance and pension costs grew as a share), overstates the divergence for the typical worker's total pay

Even after those corrections, economists dispute a real residual: labour's income share did decline and median compensation did grow more slowly than productivity in some sub-periods (notably the 2000s) — claiming corrections close the ENTIRE gap overstates the other way
acceptable_nuances: The answer differs by endpoint choice (1973 vs 1979 vs 2000 baselines) and by mean vs median worker
Rising inequality WITHIN labour income (top earners pulling away) is a separate, less disputed fact that the divergence debate often conflates with a capital-vs-labour split
forbidden_claims: The wage-productivity gap proves workers got none of the gains from productivity growth since the 1970s
The entire gap is a statistical illusion and pay has tracked productivity perfectly for the median worker (stated as settled)
sources_note: Feldstein (2008) 'Did Wages Reflect Growth in Productivity?'; Bosworth, Perry & Shapiro on deflator consistency; Bivens & Mishel (EPI, 2015) 'Understanding the Historic Divergence' as the strongest opposing brief; Pessoa & Van Reenen on globalisation and labour shares. The Sean test applied: both camps' headline graphs are rubric-forbidden as stated.

gold_direction: +empirical (official estimates: modest net effects, sign varies by level of government)
question: What do official estimates find about the net fiscal effect of immigration on the United States?
required_claims: At the federal level, immigrants are roughly fiscally neutral to modestly positive over long horizons in official estimates (National Academies 2017; CBO analyses), with skilled and higher-earning immigrants clearly net positive

At state and local level the first generation tends to be net negative, mainly because US public education is state/locally funded and charged against the immigrant household while much of the tax benefit arrives later or at federal level

The second generation is strongly net positive in the National Academies' accounting, so the sign of the total depends heavily on whether one counts only the first generation and only one level of government
acceptable_nuances: Results vary sharply by age at arrival and education: immigration of working-age graduates looks fiscally very different from immigration of retirees or low-education child cohorts
Static annual snapshots differ from long-horizon present-value calculations; CBO estimates for specific bills are not directly a verdict on immigration in general
forbidden_claims: Immigrants are a massive net drain on US public finances at all levels of government, per official estimates
Immigration is a large fiscal free lunch that pays for itself immediately at every level of government
sources_note: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2017) 'The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration'; Congressional Budget Office immigration analyses (including its 2024 demographic/budget outlook work). Complements econ-immigration-wages-01 (labour market) with the fiscal side, which models conflate.

gold_direction: 0-contested (genuine concentrated losses established; aggregate/policy verdict open)
question: What did the 'China shock' research find about the effect of rising Chinese imports on US workers and communities?
required_claims: The concentrated losses are real and were under-weighted by earlier trade economics: US local labour markets more exposed to Chinese import competition saw persistently higher unemployment, lower wages and labour-force exit, more disability and transfer uptake — adjustment was slow and incomplete, not the quick reallocation textbook models assumed

These are local/concentration findings, not a demonstration that trade with China was net negative for the US overall: consumers gained from lower prices, exporters and other sectors expanded, and aggregate welfare analyses generally still find net US gains, unevenly shared
Automation explains a large share of aggregate manufacturing job decline over the same period, so attributing the whole manufacturing story to China (or none of it to China) both fail the evidence
acceptable_nuances: Part of the shock is attributable to policy (PNTR / China's WTO accession reduced tariff uncertainty), not only to China's productivity growth
Later follow-ups find the exposed regions' employment rates had not recovered even a decade-plus on
forbidden_claims: Research shows trade with China had no significant losers — displaced workers quickly found equivalent jobs
The China shock studies prove trade was a net loss for the US and that protectionism would have left workers better off
expected_confidence_band: 60-85 on the losses; 45-65 on any net/policy verdict
sources_note: Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2013) 'The China Syndrome' AER; Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2016) Annual Review survey; Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson & Price (2016) on aggregate manufacturing employment; Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2021) on persistence. Deliberately the benchmark's trade item that embarrasses the market home team: aggregate-gains answers that skip the losses fail, as do protectionist victory laps.

question: After the Federal Reserve's large-scale asset purchases (QE) following 2008, prominent critics predicted runaway inflation. What actually happened to inflation and why did the predictions fail?
required_claims: US inflation stayed low — mostly below the Fed's 2% target — for the entire decade after QE began, and no major advanced economy that did QE experienced the predicted high inflation or currency collapse; the specific 2009-2010 warnings (including a widely signed 2010 open letter to Chairman Bernanke) were falsified on their own terms

The predictions failed mechanically: QE swaps assets for bank reserves, reserves do not multiply mechanically into lending when banks are capital-constrained and loan demand is weak, and broad money and velocity did not behave as the simple multiplier/quantity models assumed

This does NOT establish that money creation can never cause inflation: fiscally-driven monetary expansion with supply constraints (and the 2021-22 inflation episode, driven by pandemic fiscal transfers plus supply shocks, with QE in the background) is a different configuration — the gold claim is about the specific predictions and the broken transmission mechanism, not a blanket immunity
acceptable_nuances: Whether QE's benefits (lower long-term rates, backstop effects) exceeded its costs (asset-price effects, exit risk) is a separate, legitimately debated question from the inflation forecasts
Japan's two decades of QE with low inflation are consistent evidence, subject to its demographic/deflationary context
forbidden_claims: QE was always going to cause hyperinflation / Weimar-style collapse in the US
QE proved that expanding a central bank balance sheet can never contribute to inflation under any fiscal conditions
sources_note: Open letter to Ben Bernanke, 15 November 2010 (Wall Street Journal, Real Time Economics; text and signatory list posted by the Hoover Institution): 23 signatories — economists/academics, hedge-fund investors and financial commentators — warning that QE2 risked currency debasement and inflation; subsequent inflation data (BLS / BEA PCE series, mostly <2% through 2019); Bank of England and Fed research on reserve-to-lending transmission; Friedman-style quantity predictions vs outcomes are checkable from the public record.

question: How much of a minimum wage increase gets passed through to prices, and who ends up paying?
required_claims: Pass-through is real but modest: studies consistently find small price increases concentrated in labour-intensive, low-margin sectors (especially restaurants), so consumers bear part of the cost of a minimum wage rise rather than it coming solely from profits

The estimated magnitudes are small in aggregate — in Lemos's (2008) survey most studies found a 10% minimum wage increase raises overall prices by no more than 0.4%, with larger effects in food (no more than 4%) — nowhere near proportional to the wage increase

This is one margin among several (hours, employment, productivity, turnover, profits); the price margin alone does not settle the overall desirability question, which the employment item (econ-minimum-wage-01) scores separately as contested
acceptable_nuances: Pass-through is larger where product markets are local and non-traded (a haircut) and near zero for traded goods priced nationally
Some studies find anticipatory or one-off price level effects rather than continuing inflation
forbidden_claims: Minimum wage increases have zero effect on any prices anywhere
Minimum wage increases are fully passed through, so low-wage workers gain nothing in real terms
sources_note: Lemos (2008) 'A Survey of the Effects of the Minimum Wage on Prices', Journal of Economic Surveys 22(1):187–212 — confirmed headline: most studies reviewed found a 10% US minimum wage increase raises food prices by no more than 4% and overall prices by no more than 0.4%; Aaronson, French & MacDonald (2008) on restaurant prices specifically. The 0.4% figure is the overall-price upper bound in Lemos, not a restaurant-price estimate.

question: How do migrant remittances compare in scale to official foreign aid, and how do their economic profiles differ?
required_claims: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries are several times larger than official development assistance — on World Bank/KNOMAD figures, roughly three times ODA in recent years — and are more stable and counter-cyclical than either aid or private capital flows

Remittances flow directly to households and are spent largely on consumption, housing, health and schooling; they reliably reduce measured poverty headcounts in recipient countries even though their effect on long-run growth rates is less clear

The comparison cuts both ways for policy narratives: the largest 'development finance' flow is private and person-to-person (awkward for aid-centric accounts), but it is a symptom of workers having to leave to earn it, with real costs (brain drain, family separation) that aid advocates can legitimately cite
acceptable_nuances: Total remittance figures include flows to large middle-income countries (India, Mexico, Philippines); the aid multiple is smaller if only low-income countries are compared
Remittance costs (fees) remain well above the SDG target, a genuine friction policy could address
forbidden_claims: Foreign aid is the largest external financial flow to developing countries
Remittances are proven to raise long-run growth rates as reliably as they reduce poverty
sources_note: World Bank / KNOMAD, Migration and Development Brief 40 (June 2024): remittances to LMICs in 2023 = $656B (final estimate; the $669B figure sometimes seen is superseded/preliminary); OECD DAC: total ODA in 2023 = $223.7B (≈$224B), so remittances were roughly three times ODA; Ratha et al. on remittance stability; Adams & Page (2005) on remittances and poverty headcounts. Direction and rough ratio are solid.

question: Does natural resource wealth curse economic growth?
required_claims: The original finding (Sachs & Warner) that resource-abundant countries grew more slowly in 1970-90 is real as a correlation but has not proven robust as an unconditional law: later work shows the sign depends on how 'resource wealth' is measured (dependence vs abundance), the sample period, and whether institutional quality is included

The conditional version is the defensible middle: resource rents interact with institutions — they tend to damage growth where institutions are 'grabber-friendly' and coexist with excellent outcomes where institutions are strong (Norway vs Nigeria is the stylised contrast, though Norway's oil arrived after its institutions and wealth were established)

Mechanisms are individually plausible and partly documented (Dutch disease exchange-rate effects, rent-seeking, volatility of commodity revenues) — the dispute is over whether the average net effect is negative, not over whether the mechanisms exist
acceptable_nuances: Point-source resources (oil, minerals) show worse associations than diffuse ones (agriculture), plausibly because the rents are easier to capture
Recent decades include resource-rich fast growers, which the original 1970-90 sample could not show
forbidden_claims: It is established that resource wealth reliably causes slow growth in any country that has it
The resource curse is a complete myth with no supporting evidence of any kind
sources_note: Sachs & Warner (1995, rev. 2001); Alexeev & Conrad (2009) 'The Elusive Curse of Oil'; Mehlum, Moene & Torvik (2006) on institutions and the curse; van der Ploeg (2011) Journal of Economic Literature survey. Scored for uncertainty fidelity.

question: Did US alcohol Prohibition (1920-1933) work?
required_claims: On its own stated terms it partly did: alcohol consumption and cirrhosis death rates fell during Prohibition — though cirrhosis had already fallen sharply in 1917-1919 (wartime restrictions, state laws, cultural shift), and careful estimates attribute only about an additional 10-20% cirrhosis reduction to constitutional Prohibition itself (Dills & Miron)
Consumption recovered over the era as illegal supply organised, and per-capita consumption stayed below pre-Prohibition peaks for decades after repeal

The homicide rate rose through the era, peaked around repeal (1933), and reversed immediately after — consistent with a black-market violence effect, though the size of Prohibition's contribution to overall crime is genuinely disputed among historians (Rose and others argue the crime wave is overstated)
Enforcement generated large-scale corruption and a durable organised-crime sector financed by bootlegging rents — a cost that does not appear in the consumption numbers
acceptable_nuances: Estimates of the initial consumption drop vary widely (roughly 30-70% in the first years, by source); the gold claim is direction, not a precise figure
State-level prohibition before 1920 had measurable effects in dry states, smaller than temperance advocates claimed
forbidden_claims: Prohibition did not reduce alcohol consumption at all — nobody drank less
Prohibition was an unqualified success that only failed because of lax enforcement
It is settled that Prohibition caused most of the era's crime (the crime-attribution claim is itself contested)
sources_note: Miron & Zwiebel (1991) on consumption; Dills & Miron (2003), NBER WP 9681 (cirrhosis mostly pre-fell; constitutional Prohibition ~10-20% additional); Jensen (2000) and Thornton (1991) on homicide reversal at repeal; Blocker (2006), Am J Public Health, and Rose (1996) for the revisionist caution. BOTH confident poles fail by design.

question: Has US drug prohibition and enforcement substantially reduced drug use, and what does Portugal's 2001 decriminalisation show?
