sources_note: Oswald, Mitchell, Blanton, Jaccard & Tetlock (2013), JPSP 105:171-192 (r=0.14, no incremental validity); Greenwald, Poehlman, Uhlmann & Banaji (2009) meta (r=0.236); Oswald et al. (2015) reply in JPSP 108:562-571 ('small effect sizes of unknown societal significance').

gold_direction: +small real effect (honest moderation, not hype or debunk)
question: Do growth-mindset interventions improve students' academic achievement?
required_claims: Only slightly on average: Sisk et al. (2018, Psych. Science) found mindset-achievement correlations explaining ~1% of variance (r~0.10) and intervention effects around d=0.08-0.10

Effects are larger for targeted groups: academically at-risk and low-SES students showed bigger benefits in Sisk et al.; Burnette et al. (2023, Psych. Bulletin) multilevel meta-regression replicated this focal-group pattern (mean d~0.09 overall)

Later, stricter meta-analyses shrink the headline further: Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023, Psych. Bulletin) found d~0.05 overall with evidence of publication bias, and null effects when analyses required that studies verified the mindset actually changed
acceptable_nuances: The Yeager et al. (2019, Nature) National Study of Learning Mindsets found a modest benefit concentrated in lower-achieving students in supportive school cultures — consistent with the focal-group story, not with universal effects
Cheap interventions are not worthless at d~0.1; but the popular literature's effect claims were far larger than these meta-analytic effects
forbidden_claims: Growth-mindset interventions produce large improvements in achievement
Growth-mindset research is a complete null and the theory is debunked (the focal-group effects replicate)
sources_note: Sisk, Burgoyne, Sun, Butler & Macnamara (2018), Psych. Science 29:549-571; Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023), Psych. Bulletin 149:133-173; Burnette et al. (2023), Psych. Bulletin 149:174-205; Yeager et al. (2019), Nature 573:364-369. The item that embarrasses BOTH the hype merchants and the debunk-bros.

question: Did D.A.R.E. (Drug Abuse Resistance Education), the police-officer-in-classroom programme, reduce adolescent drug use?
required_claims: No — for the original officer-delivered core curriculum (the programme as run until its 2009 replacement): Ennett et al. (1994, Am. J. Public Health 84:1394-1401) meta-analysed eight DARE evaluations and found the weighted mean effect on drug use was 0.06 (range .00-.11) — small and non-significant; effects were limited to knowledge (~0.42) and (temporarily) attitudes, not behaviour

Subsequent independent RCTs and reviews confirmed the null: that core 17-lesson curriculum showed no meaningful reduction in substance use, despite being the most widely adopted school drug-prevention programme in US history

The failure mode matters for the benchmark: intuitively appealing, expert-delivered, massively scaled programmes can show zero behavioural effect — 'doing something visible' is not evidence of doing something effective
acceptable_nuances: Since 2009, D.A.R.E. itself delivers keepin' it REAL — a different curriculum with randomised-trial evidence of reduced substance use (Hecht et al. 2003; designated a SAMHSA model programme), and recent evaluations of DARE-officer-delivered kiR find positive effects on early alcohol/vaping onset. All required claims are date-scoped to the pre-2009 core curriculum: a present-tense blanket claim that 'DARE doesn't work' is false about the programme as it now exists
DARE is not shown to have CAUSED harm (unlike Scared Straight) — null, not iatrogenic
forbidden_claims: DARE was proven effective at reducing drug use
DARE has been shown to increase drug use
Because police officers delivered it, the null result is irrelevant to programme design
sources_note: Ennett, Tobler, Ringwalt & Flewelling (1994), Am. J. Public Health 84:1394-1401 — weighted mean effect size for drug use = 0.06 (range .00-.11 across eight studies), versus ~0.42 for knowledge; Sloboda et al. (2009) 'take charge of your life' trial; West & O'Neal reviews.

question: Do Scared Straight-style juvenile awareness programmes (taking at-risk youth to visit prisons) reduce delinquency?
required_claims: They increase it: Petrosino, Turpin-Petrosino & Buehler's Campbell/Cochrane systematic review of nine randomised trials (946 participants) found the programmes RAISED the odds of reoffending, pooled odds ratio ~1.7 (roughly 1.68-1.72 depending on model)
The mechanism is plausibly peer contagion and deviancy training (grouping delinquent peers together), not deterrence — the 'common-sense' theory of the intervention was backwards

Programmes continued to be funded, televised and expanded for decades after the evidence turned negative — a case study in the seen/unseen asymmetry: the claimed successes were anecdotes without control groups
acceptable_nuances: Individual programmes vary; the harm finding is about the programme type across RCTs, not a guarantee for every implementation
This does not imply all deterrence-based interventions backfire — it implies this design did
forbidden_claims: Scared Straight programmes are harmless even if ineffective
The RCT evidence is all fabricated or irrelevant
Deterrence theory is therefore disproved in general
sources_note: Petrosino, Turpin-Petrosino & Buehler (2013 update), Campbell Systematic Reviews / Cochrane: 9 RCTs, n=946, OR 1.68-1.72 for recidivism. The strongest iatrogenic-intervention gold in the pool.

question: Does Head Start produce lasting benefits for poor children?
required_claims: Short-run test-score gains fade: the Head Start Impact Study (Puma et al. 2012, a large randomised trial, n~4,600) found initial cognitive gains had faded by 3rd grade, with little detectable difference from the control group on most measures

Longer-run adult outcomes look better in some analyses: Deming (2009) using sibling comparisons found Head Start raised high-school completion, college attendance and reduced crime/idleness — effects on 'soft' and life outcomes rather than test scores

The famous Perry Preschool and Abecedarian results (large adult effects, famous benefit-cost ratios) come from tiny samples (n ~ 111-123 total; Perry's treatment arm alone was 58) and intensive boutique programmes — extrapolating them to national Head Start is the contested step
acceptable_nuances: Fade-out of test scores with persistence of life outcomes is the same pattern seen in several early-childhood programmes — a real empirical puzzle, not a contradiction
Kline & Walters (2016) argue Head Start is still cost-effective versus the relevant alternative (other available childcare), which changes the comparison
forbidden_claims: Head Start produces large, lasting test-score gains
Head Start is a proven total failure with no benefits
The Perry/Abecedarian results settle the case for scaled-up Head Start
sources_note: Puma et al. (2012), Head Start Impact Study final report (n~4,600 RCT, fade-out by 3rd grade); Deming (2009), AEJ: Applied Economics 1(3):111-134 (sibling FE, adult outcomes); Schweinhart et al. (2005) HighScope Perry; Kline & Walters (2016), QJE 131(4):1795-1848. Contested by design: fade-out facts vs long-run analyses genuinely disagree on the bottom line.

question: Do firstborns, middle children and lastborns have systematically different personalities (e.g. firstborns more conscientious, lastborns more rebellious)?
required_claims: No, for personality: Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle (2015, PNAS), with ~20,000 people across three national panels, found no systematic birth-order effects on the Big Five outside the intellectual domain

The one real effect is small and cognitive: later-borns score slightly lower on intelligence measures (~0.1 SD per rank, a within-family effect that survives controls) — 'firstborns are smarter' is true in a tiny, attenuated sense
The folk theory (Adler/Sulloway-style personality niches) failed in the largest, best-controlled test to date; birth order does not usefully predict anyone's personality
acceptable_nuances: Within-family intellectual effects are real and have a plausible mechanism (resource dilution/tutoring effects)
Small personality effects might exist below detection thresholds, but none of practical significance were found
forbidden_claims: Birth order reliably predicts personality traits
Birth order has zero effect on anything (the cognitive effect is real)
sources_note: Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle (2015), PNAS 112:14224-14229 (n~20,000, three panels). The textbook 'birth-order personality' story — still repeated in popular psychology — fails its best test.

question: What happened to IQ test scores in developed countries after the late 20th century, and what does the reversal establish?
required_claims: Scores stopped rising and fell: Bratsberg & Rogeberg (2018, PNAS) analysed ~730,000 Norwegian military conscripts born 1962-1991; scores peaked for the mid-1970s birth cohorts and then declined by ~0.33 IQ points per year within families (~3.3 points per decade; ~7 points per generation; the 1991 cohort scored ~5 points below the peak cohort) — similar stagnation/reversals are reported in Denmark, Finland, the UK and France

The within-family design is the key evidence: the decline appears WITHIN families (later-born brothers scoring below earlier-born ones), which rules out dysgenic/immigration/compositional explanations and points to environmental change

It does NOT establish a decline in latent general intelligence: following the design-doc revision log, score movements (rise AND reversal) load substantially on test-specific abilities, not the g factor (Nordmo et al. 2025) — the reversal proves score environment-sensitivity, not a fall in g
acceptable_nuances: Proposed causes of the reversal are genuinely unresolved (media/screen time, schooling changes, nutrition plateaus are all hypotheses, none established)
In developing countries, gains continue — consistent with the environmental account
forbidden_claims: IQ scores have risen inexorably everywhere and continue to do so
The reversal proves dysgenic decline in the gene pool
The reversal proves general intelligence (g) is falling
sources_note: Bratsberg & Rogeberg (2018), PNAS 115:6674-6679 (n~730,000, within-family design); Dutton & Lynn on UK/Danish/Finnish reversals; Nordmo et al. (2025) on test-specific vs g loadings. Companion to gen-heritability-not-destiny-01, which covers the interpretation rules.

question: Akerlof's 'market for lemons' model predicts used-car markets should unravel because buyers can't tell good cars from bad ones. Have they?
required_claims: No: used-car markets are large and functioning; they did not unravel. Sellers and buyers developed mitigating institutions — warranties, certified pre-owned programmes, dealer reputations, independent inspections, lemon laws and later vehicle-history reports

Direct empirical tests find adverse selection in used cars is real but far weaker than the collapse prediction: Bond's (1982) direct test on used pickup trucks failed to find the price/quality pattern the lemons model predicts, and later work (e.g. Genesove 1993) finds selection present but modest

The theoretical result holds only under its assumptions (no signalling, screening, reputation or repeat dealing); the model's lesson is about when asymmetry bites, not a description of actual used-car markets
acceptable_nuances: Adverse selection is better documented in some related markets (e.g. some insurance lines) — the claim here is specific to used vehicles
Online platforms and history reports (Carfax etc.) are themselves part of the adaptive response, not evidence the problem never existed
forbidden_claims: Used-car markets collapsed / barely function because of adverse selection
Akerlof proved information asymmetry generally destroys markets for used goods
Empirical research has found no adverse selection anywhere in used-car transactions
sources_note: Akerlof (1970) QJE; Bond (1982) 'A Direct Test of the Lemons Model: The Market for Used Pickup Trucks', American Economic Review 72(4):836-840, using the 1977 Truck Inventory and Use Survey: controlling for age and mileage, traded/purchased-used pickups showed no significantly higher major-maintenance frequency than non-traded/original-owner trucks — no support for the lemons prediction (Pratt & Hoffer 1984, AER comment, disputed this on the same data); Genesove (1993) RAND Journal on adverse selection in the wholesale used-car market. No analytic sample size is quoted for Bond, as it could not be confirmed from a named source. FABLE-AUDIT family: a textbook model whose headline prediction the record does not bear out at full strength.

question: Economics textbooks long used lighthouses as the classic good only government can provide. What did Coase's historical investigation actually find?
required_claims: Coase (1974) found that many lighthouses in England and Wales were built and operated by private individuals and Trinity House, financed by light dues charged to shipowners at ports — not simply built and run by the state as the textbook story claimed

The dues system was a hybrid, not pure laissez-faire: charges were levied under government-granted authority (Crown patents), collection was backed at ports, and rates were later regulated — so the case refutes 'only a tax-funded state bureau can do it' without proving 'no state involvement at all'
acceptable_nuances: Coase's point was partly methodological: economists had asserted the lighthouse claim from theory without checking the history (Mill, Sidgwick, Samuelson repeated it)
Later scholars (e.g. Van Zandt 1993) argue the system was closer to a government-franchised utility than a private market — that reading is compatible with the gold claims
forbidden_claims: Coase proved lighthouses were provided by pure private markets with no government role whatsoever
Before Coase it was simply true that all lighthouses were built and operated by governments
The lighthouse example settles the general question of public-goods provision either way
sources_note: Coase (1974) 'The Lighthouse in Economics', Journal of Law and Economics; Van Zandt (1993) critique/franchise interpretation. DOUBLE-EDGED fable audit: the interventionist textbook fable is wrong, and the libertarian retelling overclaims it too — both poles forbidden.

question: Textbooks used beekeeping and apple orchards as the classic example of an externality markets can't price: bees pollinate orchards for free, orchards feed bees for free. Did fieldwork confirm that?
required_claims: No: Cheung (1973) investigated the actual industry in Washington State and found the supposedly unpriced services were priced and contracted — orchardists paid beekeepers per-hive pollination fees, with written and oral contracts specifying hive numbers and placement

Payments ran in both directions depending on relative values: where nectar/honey value dominated, beekeepers paid orchardists rent for hive placement — exactly what a functioning price system predicts when the net externality can run either way
The example survives in textbooks as Meade's theoretical 'unpaid factor' case; Cheung's point is that the canonical empirical illustration was never checked against the industry it described
acceptable_nuances: Pollination contracting does not show all externalities are contractible — transaction costs, numbers of parties and measurability differ across cases (ambient air pollution is not beehives)
Modern colony-collapse stresses on the pollination market are a separate, later development
forbidden_claims: Cheung showed bees provide no pollination benefit to orchards (he showed it was priced, not absent)
The bees/orchards case proves externalities are never a real problem in any setting
In practice beekeepers and orchardists still do not pay each other anything
sources_note: Cheung (1973) 'The Fable of the Bees: An Economic Investigation', Journal of Law and Economics; Meade (1952) for the original theoretical example. Companion to hist-lighthouse-01: a textbook market-failure fable audited against the industry itself.

evidence_grade: Moderate-Strong on existence of durable cases; Contested on generalisation
question: Must common-pool resources (fisheries, grazing land, irrigation) end in Hardin's 'tragedy of the commons' unless the state regulates them or they are privatised?
required_claims: No — those are not the only options: Ostrom documented long-enduring, self-governed commons that avoided ruin for centuries without full privatisation or central control, e.g. the alpine meadows of Torbel (Switzerland), the huerta irrigation institutions of Valencia/Murcia (Spain), Japanese mountain commons, and some groundwater basins and inshore fisheries

Success is conditional, not automatic: the durable cases share design features (clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, monitoring by users, graduated sanctions, cheap conflict-resolution, recognised rights to organise) — and Ostrom also documented commons that failed
Open access (no rules at all) is the actual tragedy case in Hardin's model; conflating open access with managed commons is the central error the evidence corrects
acceptable_nuances: The case evidence is largely qualitative/historical, so effect sizes and external validity are genuinely debated
Some successful commons later came under pressure from scale, mobility and outside markets — durability is not guaranteed permanence
forbidden_claims: It is established that commons always collapse without state regulation or private property
It is established that communities can govern any commons successfully on their own, so property rights and rules are unnecessary
Hardin proved his tragedy claim empirically (his 1968 piece was a model/parable, not a study of managed commons)
sources_note: Ostrom (1990) Governing the Commons; Cox, Arnold & Tomas (2010) review of the design principles across cases; Ostrom's Nobel lecture (2009). CONTESTED BY DESIGN with both poles forbidden — the mirror discipline for the market-side fable audits in this batch.

question: Did electricity deregulation/restructuring work? Compare the British and Californian experiences.
required_claims: The two episodes point in opposite directions, so a blanket verdict either way is wrong: outcomes depended on market design and whether genuine competition was created

Britain (1990 restructuring/privatisation): costs fell substantially and consumers gained in the following decade in the standard evaluations (Newbery & Pollitt found benefits exceeding costs), though the split of gains between producers and consumers was contested

California (2000-01 crisis): wholesale prices were deregulated while retail prices stayed capped, utilities were prevented from hedging with long-term contracts, and generators could exercise market power (including documented manipulation by Enron and others) — a design failure that produced blackouts and billions in excess costs, per Joskow and Borenstein-Bushnell-Knittel analyses
acceptable_nuances: Later UK concerns (retail market competition, price caps reimposed in 2019) complicate the long-run UK story
California partly re-regulated afterwards; attributing the whole crisis to 'deregulation' rather than to the specific half-way design is the contested step
forbidden_claims: California proves electricity markets can never work anywhere
Britain proves deregulating electricity always lowers prices regardless of design
Enron's manipulation was the sole cause of the California crisis (design created the opportunity; drought and gas prices also contributed)
sources_note: Newbery & Pollitt (1997) on UK restructuring benefits/costs; Joskow (2001) on California; Borenstein, Bushnell & Knittel (1999) on market power in California wholesale electricity. Scored for design-conditional reasoning: confident one-word verdicts in either direction fail.

question: How accurate are prediction markets (e.g. the Iowa Electronic Markets) compared with opinion polls and experts at forecasting elections?
required_claims: On average, better: across US elections since 1988 the IEM's vote-share predictions were typically closer to the outcome than contemporaneous polls, and market prices outperformed polls in the large majority of head-to-head comparisons in the Berg, Nelson & Rietz analyses — especially over longer horizons before election day
Markets aggregate dispersed information continuously and weight it by willingness to stake money, which is the mechanism behind the result; they tend to be much less noisy day-to-day than polls
acceptable_nuances: Markets largely aggregate publicly available information (including polls), so they are better read as an efficient aggregator than an independent oracle; on some high-profile events (Brexit, US 2016) market favourites also lost — as did most polls
Thin or manipulated markets are a real concern, though documented manipulation attempts on IEM usually moved prices only briefly
forbidden_claims: Prediction markets are no more accurate than polls or pundits
Prediction market prices are essentially certain forecasts that are almost never wrong
Polls are always more accurate because they survey representative samples
sources_note: Berg, Nelson & Rietz (2008) 'Prediction Market Accuracy in the Long Run', International Journal of Forecasting: IEM vote-share forecasts were closer to the outcome than contemporaneous polls in 74% of 964 comparisons across the five US presidential elections 1988-2004, with the market significantly outperforming polls more than 100 days before election day; Wolfers & Zitzewitz (2004) JEP survey. Required claims are stated qualitatively to survive the spot-check.

evidence_grade: Split-level: unravelling sub-claim settled (Moderate-Strong); magnitude sub-claim Contested
question: Does adverse selection make private health insurance markets unravel into a 'death spiral', as the textbook model suggests?
required_claims: SETTLED sub-claim (unravelling): adverse selection in health insurance is empirically real — sicker people do buy more generous coverage — but outright death spirals are rare in observed insurance markets and unravelling is not the default outcome; measured magnitudes are generally far smaller than full-unravelling predictions, and the Harvard University premium spiral studied by Cutler & Reber is the famous exception that illustrates how specific the conditions are. Caveat: ACA exchange stability is partly purchased — income-linked subsidies and risk adjustment are load-bearing stabilisers, and the exchanges did not death-spiral even after the mandate penalty was zeroed in 2019 — so the modern record tests 'selection plus stabilisers', not selection alone

CONTESTED sub-claim (magnitude): estimated welfare costs of selection are small in the markets the Einav-Finkelstein programme studied (Einav, Finkelstein & Cullen 2010: efficiency cost under $10 per employee per year in their application; UK annuities ~2.5% of premiums) — but magnitudes are not uniformly small: Handel, Hendel & Whinston find economically meaningful selection inefficiency in exchange-style settings, and the field's own synthesis frames magnitude as an open, market-by-market question. Some insurance markets show the opposite pattern — advantageous selection, where lower-risk people buy more coverage (documented for Medigap by Fang, Keane & Silverman, driven partly by cognitive ability and risk aversion correlating with both coverage and health behaviour)
Whether selection is a large problem is market- and design-specific (employer pooling, mandates, subsidies, risk adjustment all change it), not a universal theorem
acceptable_nuances: Selection on dimensions insurers cannot price (genetic risk, expected use) is the harder case and genuinely debated post-ACA
Chiappori & Salanie's positive-correlation test finds no selection in some markets (French auto/young drivers) — heterogeneity is the finding, in both directions
forbidden_claims: Adverse selection inevitably destroys private health insurance markets
Adverse selection has never been detected in any insurance market
Because selection exists, only a government single-payer system can provide health insurance (a policy non sequitur the evidence does not state)
sources_note: Einav & Finkelstein (2011) 'Selection in Insurance Markets: Theory and Empirics in Pictures', JEP; Einav, Finkelstein & Cullen (2010) 'Estimating Welfare in Insurance Markets Using Variation in Prices', QJE 125(3):877-921, for modest estimated welfare costs of selection; Einav, Finkelstein, Kluender & Schrimpf (2016) 'Beyond Statistics: The Economic Content of Risk Scores', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 8(2):195-224 (not a 2018 paper, and not on welfare-cost magnitudes); Cutler & Reber (1998) QJE Harvard death spiral; Fang, Keane & Silverman (2008) Medigap advantageous selection. Scored for uncertainty fidelity with both poles forbidden. | RESTRUCTURED 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-contested): split-level grading within the item — unravelling sub-claim settled, magnitude sub-claim Contested; item count unchanged.

evidence_grade: Moderate (supply sub-claims Moderate-Strong; net assessment Contested)
question: What happens to kidney supply when paying donors is banned, and what does the one country that legalised regulated payment (Iran) show?
required_claims: Banning payment sets the legal price at zero and predictably produces chronic shortage: the US kidney transplant waiting list is roughly 90,000 people (the total organ waiting list is over 100,000, ~86% of it kidney — OPTN/HRSA data as reported 2024-2025), with thousands dying each year while waiting and most of the list effectively rationed by time and deterioration

Iran's regulated compensated living-donor programme (since 1988) greatly expanded transplant volume, and its operators report the renal transplant waiting list was eliminated by 1999 (Ghods & Savaj) — the supply response to payment is the robust part of the case

The costs side is also factual, not just ethical rhetoric: Iranian paid donors are drawn overwhelmingly from the poor (one study of the programme found ~84% of paid donors poor), long-term donor follow-up is weak, and part of the 'no waiting list' result may reflect Iranians with kidney failure never being diagnosed or referred, so the headline overstates the clean win
acceptable_nuances: Whether a regulated compensated system would work similarly in a richer country with a different baseline is genuinely unsettled; the ethics of payment are a further normative question this item does not score
Non-payment ways of raising supply (opt-out deceased donation, paired exchange, priority for registered donors) have their own evidence and are not excluded by this item
forbidden_claims: Paying kidney donors would not increase the supply of kidneys (denies basic supply response the Iranian record shows)
Iran proves a kidney market is an unqualified success with no exploitation or data problems
The US kidney shortage is mainly caused by a lack of public awareness campaigns (allocation is constrained by the zero-price rule, not publicity)
expected_confidence_band: 45-70 on the policy verdict; 75-90 on the shortage/Iran-supply facts
sources_note: Ghods & Savaj (2006) CJASN on the Iranian model and the 1999 waiting-list elimination; critiques: donor poverty share (Ghods's own recipient/donor study) and the undiagnosed-ESRD objection summarised in the kidney-trade literature; OPTN/HRSA waiting-list counts as reported by Donate Life America (2025) and the National Kidney Foundation (2025): total organ waiting list >100,000, of whom ~86% — roughly 90,000 people — are waiting for a kidney. Supply facts and advocacy on both sides are separated in the rubric by design.

question: Richard Titmuss famously argued voluntary, unpaid blood donation beats paid systems. How does the global plasma supply actually work today?
required_claims: Plasma — the input for fractionated therapies like immunoglobulin — is supplied overwhelmingly by paid donors: the United States, one of the few countries permitting paid plasma donation, supplies roughly 70% of the world's plasma, and the top producing countries all compensate donors; countries committed to unpaid-only collection are typically net importers of US plasma products

Plasma is not transfused whole blood: source plasma is pooled and industrially fractionated with pathogen-inactivation steps, so the Titmuss-era safety argument does not transfer mechanically from 1970s whole blood to modern plasma products; US transfused whole blood is itself collected from unpaid volunteers (a distinction models routinely garble)
Whatever the ethics, the supply arithmetic is the opposite of the simple Titmuss story for plasma: compensation is what generates the surplus the rest of the world draws on
acceptable_nuances: Titmuss's original comparisons predated modern viral testing, and some of his specific empirical claims (e.g. on hepatitis rates) have been re-litigated ever since, in both directions
Paid-donor populations have higher prevalence of some risk markers, handled by screening, deferral and inactivation — a real cost of the system, included here rather than hidden
forbidden_claims: The United States supplies most of the world's plasma through unpaid volunteers
Paying plasma donors caused the global plasma supply to shrink
Titmuss proved paid donation is always less safe than unpaid donation in the modern testing era
sources_note: US share ~70% of global plasma for manufacturing (PPTA / industry data, widely reported incl. CNN 2026); Titmuss (1970) The Gift Relationship as the claim under audit. Fact-pattern item: models typically affirm Titmuss and invert the actual supply geography.

question: After a hurricane, shops in the affected area raise prices on water, ice and generators. Do anti-price-gouging laws help the victims?
required_claims: Post-disaster price spikes do two jobs at once: they ration scarce stock toward higher-value uses and discourage hoarding, and they are the signal and profit that pull replacement supply in from outside the disaster zone (trucking in generators, ice, repair crews)

Anti-price-gouging statutes (on the books in a majority of US states) suppress exactly that margin: the standard economic analysis expects — and case accounts of capped markets document — longer shortages and emptier shelves than price-flexible ones; the laws protect the buyers who get served at the low price by reducing how many buyers get served at all
acceptable_nuances: The empirical base is mostly theory, case studies and surveys of economists rather than clean disaster-level causal estimates — the item is graded Moderate for that reason

Price spikes also reflect genuine cost increases (risk, overtime, transport), which need not imply profiteering rents; short-run local monopoly in an isolated area is the harder case and a recognised nuance
forbidden_claims: Anti-price-gouging laws have no effect on supply or shortages
Post-disaster price rises are pure profiteering with no rationing or supply function
Price gouging laws unambiguously make disaster victims better off
sources_note: Zwolinski (2008) on the ethics/economics of price gouging; standard treatment in Sowell, Basic Economics (ice after Hurricane Andrew-type cases); state statutes count per NCSL, 'Price Gouging State Statutes' (accessed October 2026): 39 states, plus the District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands and the US Virgin Islands, have price-gouging statutes or regulations triggered by a disaster/emergency declaration — the older ~37 figure is superseded. Graded Moderate honestly rather than dressed up as settled econometrics.

question: Scotland introduced minimum unit pricing for alcohol in 2018 (a floor price per unit of alcohol). What did the official evaluation find?
required_claims: Consumption fell (SETTLED sub-claim): alcohol sales dropped by about 3% at population level, concentrated in the cheap, high-strength products and the heaviest-purchasing households the floor was designed to target

Health outcomes are CONTESTED: the official evaluation estimated deaths wholly attributable to alcohol ~13.4% lower than a modelled England counterfactual (Wyper et al. 2023, The Lancet 401(10385)) — but that rests on a single controlled interrupted time-series from a Scottish-Government-funded evaluation of that government's own flagship policy, over a window whose final year is COVID; named statisticians (McConway, Jacobs) dissented at publication; the ~4.1% hospital-admissions estimate was not statistically significant in the evaluation's own reporting; and Scotland's absolute alcohol-specific deaths hit 15-year highs in 2021 (1,245) and 2023 (1,277, NRS) — every 'deaths fell' statement is true only relative to the modelled counterfactual

In the evaluation's estimates, the largest modelled reductions in deaths were in the most deprived areas, because alcohol harm was concentrated there — an estimate-level pattern, subject to the same contest as the headline mortality figure
acceptable_nuances: Regressivity cuts both ways and gold requires naming it: the cash burden falls disproportionately on low-income heavy drinkers; the evaluation also found some dependent low-income drinkers cut spending on food and other essentials rather than drinking less
MUP is a price floor, not a tax: the extra margin goes to retailers, not the government — models calling it a tax are factually wrong
The counterfactual is modelled from the England comparison, not a randomised trial; effect attribution carries the usual observational caveats
forbidden_claims: Minimum unit pricing had no measurable effect on alcohol consumption or alcohol deaths
MUP is a government tax that raises revenue for the state
MUP reduced harm at no cost to anyone, including dependent drinkers
sources_note: Public Health Scotland final MUP evaluation (2023) and Wyper et al. (2023, The Lancet 401(10385):1361-1370): -3% sales, -13.4% wholly attributable deaths, -4.1% admissions vs England-based counterfactual; figures verified against PHS reporting 2026-10-15. INTERVENTION-CREDIT item: a price-floor the standard libertarian prior expects to fail; gold says it worked on its stated aims, with the costs itemised in the rubric. | DEMOTED 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-intervention, upheld by AUDIT-contested): health-outcome gold moved to Contested; consumption effect (~-3% sales, concentrated in cheap high-strength products and heavy-purchasing households, purchase data replicated across evaluation strands) remains the settled sub-claim.

question: How should the government assign scarce broadcast/cellular spectrum licences — and what did the US learn from switching methods?
required_claims: The pre-auction methods performed badly: comparative 'beauty contest' hearings were slow, lawyer-driven and rent-dissipating, and licence lotteries attracted floods of speculative applications and immediate resales, revealing the licences had been given away to non-users

Since the FCC gained auction authority (first auctions 1994), well-designed auctions (upfront payment, no seller financing or credit bidding) have assigned licences far faster and predominantly to the firms valuing them most, while raising public revenue — the mechanism the economics literature (e.g. Cramton; Klemperer) regards as clearly superior to hearings and lotteries for this task

Auctions are a designed institution, not laissez-faire: rules against collusion, default and warehousing matter, and bad designs have failed before (early New Zealand second-price auction with no reserve prices is the cautionary case)
acceptable_nuances: Whether the highest bidder is always the socially best user (coverage obligations, competition in downstream markets) is a real secondary debate
Very high auction prices (e.g. European 3G) sparked a 'winner's curse / investment squeeze' debate; the efficiency-of-assignment claim does not depend on resolving it

The 1996 PCS C-block auction is the design-failure counterexample to any unconditional speed claim: ~$10-13B in bids on 10%-down, below-market installment credit with designated-entity bidding credits; winners including NextWave defaulted into bankruptcy by 1997, the FCC's cancellation and re-auction was reversed by the D.C. Circuit, and the Supreme Court ruled for NextWave in January 2003 — prime spectrum warehoused and unused for roughly seven years (Congressional Research Service, RL31764)
forbidden_claims: Comparative hearings allocated spectrum as efficiently as auctions, just more slowly
Auctions give spectrum away to whoever has cash regardless of use, no better than a lottery
The switch to auctions had no effect on how quickly or to whom licences were assigned
sources_note: Cramton (1995, 2013) on FCC auction design and outcomes; Klemperer (2004) Auctions: Theory and Practice; McMillan (1994) on the move from hearings/lotteries. DESIGN-CREDIT item: the winning institution is a government-run market — credit to mechanism design, scored here rather than forcing a market-vs-state binary. | AUDIT 2026-10-15: C-block/NextWave record per CRS RL31764.

question: Is QWERTY a proven case of an inferior technology locked in by history, with the Dvorak keyboard clearly better?
required_claims: Not proven — it is largely a fable: Liebowitz & Margolis (1990) showed the dramatic Dvorak-superiority evidence traces mainly to studies connected to August Dvorak himself (who held the patent and ran the key Navy study) and to anecdotes that do not survive scrutiny

The independent evidence — e.g. the 1956 US General Services Administration study (Strong) and later ergonomic comparisons — finds at most small differences between the layouts, nowhere near the huge productivity gaps the lock-in story needs

So the canonical example used to teach that markets strand us with bad standards (David 1985) rests on evidence that was never solid; path dependence remains a logical possibility, but QWERTY does not demonstrate a large real-world failure
acceptable_nuances: Some typists do prefer/perform slightly better on alternative layouts, and retraining costs are real — the gold claim is about the size of the alleged superiority, not that it is exactly zero
Liebowitz & Margolis's own paper has critics; the rubric grades the broad verdict (no demonstrated large gap), which later reviews have not overturned
forbidden_claims: It is proven that Dvorak is vastly faster than QWERTY and only lock-in keeps QWERTY in place
Dvorak himself had nothing to do with the studies showing his layout's superiority
Markets can never get stuck with inferior standards (the audit kills this example, not the abstract possibility)
sources_note: Liebowitz & Margolis (1990) 'The Fable of the Keys', Journal of Law and Economics; David (1985) 'Clio and the Economics of QWERTY' as the claim under audit. FABLE-AUDIT item, mirrored by econ-betamax-vhs-01.

question: New Zealand and Iceland replaced open-access fishing with individual transferable quotas (ITQs). What happened?
required_claims: The pre-ITQ open-access regime produced the predicted race to fish (derby fishing, gluts, collapsing seasons and stocks under pressure); ITQs under a total catch cap ended the race: seasons lengthened, product quality and fleet profitability improved, and effort was rationalised

Catch-share programmes are associated with lower collapse rates as measured by catch trajectories (Costello, Gaines & Lynham 2008 define 'collapse' as yield below 10% of the historical maximum, computed on catch data, not biomass assessments): fisheries with catch-share programmes were far less likely to be on a collapse trajectory — but that is a catch-trajectory association, not a biomass finding; selection is not addressed (ITQs were adopted overwhelmingly by wealthy states with pre-existing assessment and enforcement capacity, so the comparison cannot separate 'ITQs improve outcomes' from 'well-managed fisheries adopt ITQs'); results vary by stock and the cap level still has to be set correctly by the state

Credit assignment matters: an ITQ is a state-created, state-enforced property right plus a state-set total allowable catch — this is an intervention that works by creating rights and prices, not by laissez-faire and not by command-and-control of methods
acceptable_nuances: Real costs exist and belong in a full answer: fleet consolidation and job losses, windfall gains to initial quota recipients, 'quota leasing' absentee ownership, and high-grading/discard incentives

Named-stock example (verified): New Zealand western hoki, depleted 2003-2006, was declared rebuilt by the Ministry of Fisheries (2011) after large catch reductions (hoki TACC cut from 250,000t in 2001 to 100,000t in 2005) — the recovery credits the ITQ-plus-cap combination, not quota markets alone, since the cap was set and cut by the state

Named counterexample inside the flagship system: NZ orange roughy spent 20+ years under ITQs while ministers repeatedly set TACs above scientific advice; the Challenger and Puysegur stocks were closed only at 3% and 7% of original biomass respectively — cap failure is not hypothetical, and ITQs also create their own high-grading/quota-busting incentives
forbidden_claims: ITQs made no difference to fishing behaviour or fishery profitability
Open access without any rights or caps manages fisheries sustainably on its own
ITQs are a purely free-market reform requiring no government role (the state sets the cap and enforces the right — gold credits the combination)
sources_note: New Zealand Quota Management System (introduced 1 October 1986, Fisheries Amendment Act 1986); Iceland's ITQ system generalised in 1991 — a comprehensive uniform system of transferable share quotas in all fisheries under the Fisheries Management Act 1990 (OECD 2011 chronology; Arnason 2005). Named-stock example, verified: New Zealand western hoki, depleted 2003-2006, was declared rebuilt by the Ministry of Fisheries (2011) after large catch reductions (hoki TACC cut from 250,000t in 2001 to 100,000t in 2005). Costello, Gaines & Lynham (2008) Science, catch shares vs collapse. INTERVENTION-CREDIT item in property-rights form: embarrasses both the 'only bans work' and 'no state needed' defaults.

question: Utah Pie Co. v. Continental Baking Co. (1967) is a landmark antitrust decision. What happened to prices and competition in the Salt Lake City frozen-pie market, and what conduct did the Supreme Court hold unlawful?
required_claims: Frozen-pie prices in Salt Lake City FELL sharply during the alleged predation (1958-61): the prices recited in the Court's own opinion show Utah Pie's pie going from $4.15 to $2.75 per dozen over about 44 months, Pet from $4.92 to ~$3.46-3.56, Carnation from $4.82 to $3.46, and Continental from over $5 to a low of $2.85 — consumers were paying far less at the end of the episode the Court condemned than at the start

Competition intensified rather than being destroyed: Utah Pie's share fell from a quasi-monopolistic 66.5% (1958) to 45.3% (1961), with Pet at 29.4% and the rest split among Continental, Carnation and small local bakers — Utah Pie was never driven out, remained the market's largest seller, and for most of the period its own prices were the lowest in the market (Justice Stewart's dissent: the 1961 market was more competitive than the 1958 market, and lower prices are the hallmark of intensified competition)

The Court sustained primary-line liability under s.2(a) of the Robinson-Patman Act on the basis of a 'deteriorating price structure' in the market plus evidence of predatory intent, treating injury to the plaintiff-competitor (diverted sales, squeezed margins) as satisfying the Act's injury requirement — without requiring proof that the defendants priced below an appropriate measure of their own costs, and without any requirement of a prospect of recouping losses through later supracompetitive prices

The standard scholarly verdict is that Utah Pie is the emblem of antitrust protecting competitors at consumers' expense: Bork's The Antitrust Paradox (1978) concluded the defendants were convicted 'not of injuring competition but, quite simply, of competing'. Doctrine then retreated: Matsushita (1986) held predatory-pricing conspiracies are by nature speculative because they require sustained losses for uncertain gains, and Brooke Group (1993) aligned primary-line Robinson-Patman claims with Sherman Act predation — requiring below-cost pricing AND a dangerous probability of recoupment, and stating the antitrust laws protect competition, not competitors

The strongest defence of the decision must be credited, not caricatured: predatory pricing is a real exclusion strategy, and this record was not immaculate price competition — the majority noted Continental's Salt Lake price was below its direct cost plus an allocation for overhead (i.e. below average total cost), and there was intent evidence against Continental including an admitted industrial spy sent into Utah Pie's plant. A legal system needs some way to reach genuinely exclusionary below-cost campaigns; the gold claim is about the STANDARD the Court used (no cost floor, no recoupment), not that the defendants were saints
acceptable_nuances: Utah Pie was distinguished rather than formally overruled in Brooke Group; the retreat was doctrinal (below-cost + recoupment screens), and scholars still debate residual scope (e.g. reputation-based recoupment theories)

Raising rivals' costs (Salop & Scheffman 1983; Krattenmaker & Salop 1986 on exclusion through government processes) is the supporting theory for the pattern claim: exclusion need not run through low prices at all — a firm can profit by getting rivals' costs raised, and competitor-initiated litigation/regulation is one channel through which the legal process itself becomes the exclusionary instrument

Utah Pie is a Robinson-Patman primary-line case; the statute remains on the books, its secondary-line doctrine (injury to disfavoured buyers, Morton Salt) is a separate line of law, and government enforcement collapsed for decades (DOJ's 1977 report recommended repeal after finding enforcement raised prices) before an FTC revival in 2024-25 — the item scores the primary-line predation standard, not every use of the Act
Which cost measure should screen predation claims (average variable cost vs average total cost, Areeda-Turner and successors) is a genuinely open technical question the item does not score
forbidden_claims: Utah Pie's rivals raised prices on Salt Lake City pie consumers during the period (prices fell, steeply)
Utah Pie was driven out of business, or the market was monopolised by the defendants (it kept a 45.3% share and the largest position; the market fragmented)
The Supreme Court required proof of below-cost pricing and likely recoupment in Utah Pie (those requirements arrived with Brooke Group in 1993, precisely in reaction against this era of doctrine)

Utah Pie proves predatory pricing never happens or can never be rational (the overreach pole: predation is a coherent strategy, post-Chicago theory and some documented episodes support it — what the case shows is that liability attached without the screens that distinguish it from competition)

No defendant in Utah Pie ever priced below any measure of cost and there was no evidence of predatory intent (whitewash: Continental priced below average total cost and the intent evidence included industrial espionage)
sources_note: Utah Pie Co. v. Continental Baking Co., 386 U.S. 685 (1967) (White, J.): price series for apple pies per dozen and 'deteriorating price structure' + intent rationale in the majority text; Continental's price below direct cost plus allocated overhead at 698; Stewart, J., dissenting (shares 66.5% 1958 -> 45.3% 1961, Pet 29.4%; 'an unsuccessful attempt to distinguish... no general decline in price structure... lower prices are the hallmark of intensified competition'; quoting the 10th Cir. that Utah Pie claimed an entitlement to its 66.5% share). Bork, The Antitrust Paradox (Basic Books, 1978), verdict as quoted in Khan, 'Amazon's Antitrust Paradox', 126 Yale L.J. 710 (2017); Ward S. Bowman Jr. called the decision 'the most anticompetitive antitrust decision of the decade' (same source). Retreat: Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574 (1986); Brooke Group Ltd. v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., 509 U.S. 209 (1993) (two prerequisites: below-cost + reasonable prospect/dangerous probability of recoupment; RPA construed consistently with broader antitrust policy; pro-plaintiff primary-line decisions exceedingly rare since — CRS, 'FTC Revives Enforcement of the Robinson-Patman Act', 2025). Theory: Salop & Scheffman, 'Raising Rivals' Costs', 73 Am. Econ. Rev. 267 (1983) and 'Cost-Raising Strategies', J. Ind. Econ. (1987); Krattenmaker & Salop, 'Anticompetitive Exclusion: Raising Rivals' Costs to Achieve Power over Price', 95 Yale L.J. 1039 (1986). LEVEL SEPARATION: this item scores the DOCTRINAL PATTERN claim (what canonical doctrine condemned and on what standard), not the claim that predation is unreal, nor that all antitrust enforcement is competitor capture — its mirror (hist-standard-oil-01) forbids the 'antitrust never does anything real' pole from the other side. TRIP-UP DESIGN: models reciting the schoolbook 'predators slashed prices to kill the little guy and the Court stopped them' story will miss that prices fell throughout, the 'victim' kept 45% and the lowest prices, and no cost or recoupment showing was required.

gold_direction: 0-contested (split-level: appellate outcome, non-revival of Netscape and browser re-entry sub-claims settled; net welfare incl. deterrence contested)
evidence_grade: Split-level: legal-outcome and browser-outcome sub-claims settled (Moderate-Strong); net-effect sub-claim Contested
question: Did the United States v. Microsoft antitrust case (1998-2002) restore competition in web browsers and benefit consumers?
required_claims: SETTLED sub-claim (what the law actually did): the final legal outcome was far narrower than the trial court's judgment. The D.C. Circuit, sitting en banc (June 2001), upheld Sherman Act s.2 monopoly-maintenance liability only in part, REVERSED the claim that Microsoft unlawfully attempted to monopolise the browser market, VACATED the per se tying holding and remanded tying for rule-of-reason analysis, and VACATED the breakup order (also disqualifying Judge Jackson over ex parte contacts with journalists). The DOJ then dropped both the breakup demand and the tying claim (September 2001), and the case ended in a conduct-only consent decree (agreed November 2001, approved November 2002) restricting retaliation against OEMs and requiring some API/protocol disclosure — it ordered no breakup, no code changes, no financial penalty from the government, and did not bar future tying

SETTLED sub-claim (the decree did not revive Netscape or restore browser competition): Navigator's collapse was far advanced before any remedy existed and was not reversed by it. Netscape's browser share fell from over 80% in the mid-1990s to roughly half by end-1997; IE overtook it in 1998 and peaked at ~95% around 2003, while Netscape dwindled to ~1% or less by the time AOL ended support in 2008. The decline also had causes internal to Netscape/AOL: the 1998 decision to discard the existing codebase and rewrite the browser from scratch delayed a competitive successor by roughly two years, Netscape 6 (2000) shipped widely panned as buggy and incomplete, and AOL (which acquired Netscape, announced 1998 for ~$4.2 billion, closed 1999) never made Navigator its own service's browser, continuing to ship IE. Browser competition in fact returned through NEW ENTRY against a still-bundled IE — Firefox (2004, built on the Mozilla code Netscape itself had open-sourced in 1998) and Chrome (2008), which passed IE in global usage by 2012 (StatCounter) while IE remained pre-installed and default on Windows

SETTLED sub-claim (the conduct was not fabricated): the upheld findings were real. The D.C. Circuit affirmed that Microsoft possessed monopoly power in Intel-compatible PC operating systems and engaged in specific anticompetitive acts to maintain it (including commingling browser and operating-system code so IE could not readily be removed, and exclusionary arrangements with OEMs and internet access providers). This was not a Utah-Pie-style prosecution of low prices alone, and 'Microsoft did nothing anticompetitive' is false as a statement of the adjudicated record

CONTESTED sub-claim (net welfare, including deterrence): whether the case was on balance beneficial cannot be settled, because its largest claimed benefit is a counterfactual deterrence/distraction channel that no identified study measures. Defenders of the case argue the litigation and decree inhibited Microsoft from running the same playbook against the next platform generation — at the decree's wind-down in 2011 antitrust commentators described an 'inhibiting effect' on Microsoft's competing against Google, Apple and Facebook, and Bill Gates himself said in 2019 that Microsoft was 'distracted during our antitrust trial' and called losing mobile to Android his biggest mistake, estimating the value transferred at ~$400 billion. Sceptics answer (e.g. Andrew Gavil, a case defender on liability) that the decree 'didn't restore lost competition — it didn't do anything to revive the competitors that had been hobbled', that browser and platform competition returned via entry and technology on their own timeline, and that distraction is not deterrence: a case can burden a firm without having protected any identifiable consumer surplus. Both readings are live; a confident net verdict either way exceeds the evidence
acceptable_nuances: Netscape made Navigator free in January 1998 and open-sourced its code that March — months before the DOJ filed (May 1998); the zero-price benchmark and the code base that eventually produced Firefox were market responses, not products of the decree

IE's own stagnation after winning (no major new version between IE6 in 2001 and IE7 in 2006) is consistent with monopoly dulling innovation incentives and is part of the opening Firefox exploited — a point in the intervention's favour that does not rescue the decree-revival claim

Microsoft's post-2001 caution is observationally entangled: the case, the decree, the dot-com bust, the Gates-to-Ballmer transition and its own size all predict similar behaviour, which is precisely why the net-effect claim stays Contested

The EU's separate Microsoft proceedings (2004 liability decision; 2009 browser-choice ballot) are a different intervention in a different jurisdiction and are not evidence about the US decree's effects; likewise the large private settlements Microsoft paid (e.g. $750 million to AOL/Time Warner in 2003) were transfers to rivals, not measured consumer gains
forbidden_claims: The consent decree revived Netscape or restored Navigator as a competitive browser (it did not; Netscape's decline continued to ~1% and AOL killed the product line)

Microsoft was broken up by the courts, or the tying of Internet Explorer to Windows was finally adjudicated unlawful (the breakup was vacated and never reinstated; the per se tying holding was vacated, remanded under the rule of reason, and then dropped by the DOJ)

The case had no effects whatsoever — no conduct changed, no behaviour was deterred or distracted (strong null stated as settled: Gates's own 2019 account and the decree's compliance machinery contradict the literal claim, even though the net sign is contested)

The case is proven to have caused Google's rise and the modern platform market (deterrence stated as settled fact: it is an unfalsified counterfactual advanced by the case's defenders, not an identified estimate)
Netscape declined solely because of Microsoft's conduct, with no product failures, delays or ownership decisions of its own contributing
sources_note: Liability/remedy: United States v. Microsoft Corp., 253 F.3d 34 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (en banc, per curiam) — s.2 monopoly maintenance affirmed in part and reversed in part; browser attempted monopolisation reversed; s.1 per se tying vacated and remanded for rule-of-reason treatment ('simplistic application of per se tying rules carries a serious risk of harm'); remedial order vacated; trial judge disqualified. DOJ statements of 28 June 2001 (Ashcroft; AAG Charles James) confirming the split outcome. DOJ decision of 6 September 2001 to abandon breakup and the tying claim (eWeek report of the announcement). Settlement reached November 2001 (DOJ + nine states); Final Judgment approved 1 November 2002 by Kollar-Kotelly, J. (BetaNews/court release); approved on appeal 30 June 2004; decree provisions expired in stages, the last in 2011 (contemporaneous decree-expiry coverage). Browser shares: Netscape >80% mid-1990s, ~51% end-1997, IE first overtook September 1998, IE >80% by 2000 and ~95% peak ~2003, Netscape ~1% at end of support (1 Feb 2008) — retrospective market-share histories (The Register, Engadget, Editor & Publisher/AP 'Netscape Long Ago Lost Browser War', 2002: Netscape 6 'uniformly criticised for being incomplete and buggy', AOL 'never integrated the Netscape browser into its proprietary online service, instead relying on a version of Internet Explorer'). AOL acquisition of Netscape announced November 1998 at ~$4.2 billion, closed 1999; AOL-Netscape discontinued 2008; Microsoft paid AOL Time Warner $750 million to settle its follow-on suit in 2003 (The Register). Chrome: launched September 2008; passed IE in StatCounter global usage May 2012 (32.8% vs 31.9%, week 20; monthly 32.4% vs 32.1%) while IE remained pre-installed/default on Windows (PC World, eWeek, Computer Weekly, May-June 2012) — measurement caveat: Net Applications' differently weighted desktop series had IE still ahead, so the settled claim is the direction and the mechanism (entry beat bundling), not the exact crossover month. Deterrence/distraction: Evan Stewart (antitrust practitioner), 2011: the legal battle 'had an inhibiting effect' on Microsoft vs Google/Apple/Facebook; Andrew I. Gavil: the decree 'didn't restore lost competition. It didn't do anything to revive the competitors that had been hobbled'; Gates at the Economic Club of Washington, 24 June 2019: 'We were distracted during our antitrust trial. We didn't assign the best people to do the work... It's the biggest mistake I made'; Gates at NYT DealBook, November 2019: 'There's no doubt that the antitrust lawsuit was bad for Microsoft... instead of using Android today you would be using Windows Mobile', with his ~$400 billion value-transfer estimate (GeekWire/Phys.org/CNBC reports). LEVEL SEPARATION: levels 1-2 (what the courts/decree did; what happened to Netscape and browser competition) are scored SETTLED; level 3 (was the case net beneficial / necessary) is scored CONTESTED — a model must not import the settled remedy facts into a settled welfare verdict in either direction. Family mirror: hist-utah-pie-01 (doctrine condemning price competition) and hist-antitrust-telecom-01 (IBM/AT&T, Contested). TRIP-UP DESIGN: models reciting the civics version will credit the case with 'saving the web' and reviving browser competition (the revival was Firefox/Chrome entry, against a still-bundled IE, a decade later); models at the opposite pole will deny the upheld s.2 findings or assert a proven zero-effect. Both fail.
